subtopic: APPLICATION TO CERTAIN MEMBERS OF CANADIAN AND UNITED KINGDOM FORCES-CHANGES IN PRINCIPLE AND PROCEDURE

speechtext:
Hon. IAN A. MACKENZIE (Minister of Pensions and National Health) moved that the house go into committee on Bill No. 17, to amend the Pension Act.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Fournier (Hull) in the chair.
On section 1-Definitions.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. HANSON (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: APPLICATION TO CERTAIN MEMBERS OF CANADIAN AND UNITED KINGDOM FORCES-CHANGES IN PRINCIPLE AND PROCEDURE
speechtext:
The question of pensions is one that heretofore during my experience in this house has always been given the most careful consideration by all bodies of opinion in the house. For the most part, so far as I can recall, proposed amendments to the Pension Act have always been referred to a special committee made up almost entirely, if not altogether, of ex-service men. Those of us who do not- fall within that category have in large measure depended upon the wisdom with which these men have handled the situation. Personally I know very little in practice of the workings and operation of the Pension Act. But I understand that it is an intricate ' subject and that it has been a matter of intensive study now over a period of at least twenty-five years.
On its face the bill as brought down by the minister some months ago appeared to be quite understandable. But as brought back with the report of the committee it contains several extensions, and if I apprehend aright after a hurried reading of it this morning it proposes an extension of certain principles and perhaps the introduction of some new ones. Therefore I think it would be very helpful to the committee if the minister would make a considered statement of the position-what was intended by the bill, what its provisions were before it went to the committee, what changes have been effected by the committee,
Pension Act

and generally the scope of the amendments and the whole present intent of the measure. Will he also let us know whether the committee was unanimous. He might also take the committee into his confidence and state in terms of dollars and cents what obligations may be incurred by the treasury under the present proposals, so that the country may have a real understanding of the position.
Hon. IAN A. MACKENZIE (Minister of Pensions and National Health): I am glad indeed to accede to the very reasonable request of my hon. friend. To answer fully I must deal briefly with some of the essential principles and provisions of pension legislation.
I would remind my hon. friend that when the war broke out immediately by order in council of September 2, 1939, the provisions and principles of the then existing pension legislation in Canada were made applicable to all serving in the Canadian forces. That remained in effect for some months, until certain cases arose which cast some doubt upon the wisdom of the application of what might be called the absolute insurance principle to all those who were serving in the forces, whether in Canada or overseas.
As a result of some of these cases coming to the notice of the government a departmental committee was set up to investigate the situation. I shall quote one or two paragraphs from their report:
The question arises whether this assumption of liability on the part of the state is a justifiable and proper one under the present circumstances, and whether the application of such a general principle of insurance against practically all risks should be applied without discrimination to all members of the forces.
The committee feel that where a citizen voluntarily enlists for war service and in the course of such service leaves Canada, he and his dependents are in a different category from those who serve in Canada only. This basic differentiation underlies the consideration of the terms of reference outlined. . , .
The committee feel that there can be little argument against the state providing compensation to a man or his dependents for any disease, injury or death which arises out of or is caused by the performance of his duties.
This latter principle is the one applied in the Pension Act to service in the armed forces during peace. Subsequent to that report another order in council was passed on May 21, 1940, the vital paragraph being as follows:
Pension shall be granted for service in Canada-"when the injury or disease or aggravation thereof, resulting in disability or death, in respect of which the application for pension is made, was attributable to military service as such."
In other words the order in council of May 21, 1940, definitely restricted the order in council of September 2, 1929.
IMr. R. B. Hanson.]

subtopic: APPLICATION TO CERTAIN MEMBERS OF CANADIAN AND UNITED KINGDOM FORCES-CHANGES IN PRINCIPLE AND PROCEDURE
speechtext:
But it
extended the theatre of war to Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: APPLICATION TO CERTAIN MEMBERS OF CANADIAN AND UNITED KINGDOM FORCES-CHANGES IN PRINCIPLE AND PROCEDURE
speechtext: It applied to service in Canada; that is correct.

subtopic: APPLICATION TO CERTAIN MEMBERS OF CANADIAN AND UNITED KINGDOM FORCES-CHANGES IN PRINCIPLE AND PROCEDURE
speechtext: And did it apply to the reserve forces of the Canadian Army?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: APPLICATION TO CERTAIN MEMBERS OF CANADIAN AND UNITED KINGDOM FORCES-CHANGES IN PRINCIPLE AND PROCEDURE
speechtext:
It applied at that time to all forces serving in Canada; and the insurance principle, which after many years of variation by legislation became the final principle of the old act as applied to the forces of the great war, was abandoned by that order in council so far as service in Canada was concerned. Then we had the next step, the introduction of the original bill 17, not the amended bill as we have it to-day. The essential section of bill 17, dealing with this very principle, was section 5, subsection 2, under which pension was payable for service in Canada-

when an injury or disease or aggravation thereof resulting in disability or death in respect of which the application for pension is made arose out of and was directly connected with such military or war service, as the case may be.
In our judgment these words are not so restrictive as were the words of the order in council of May 21. 1940; and as these words now appear in subsection 2 of section 6 of the amended bill, the word "and" becomes "or," so there is an alternative and it is made broader still.
In regard to the history of the insurance principle, all those who are familiar with pension legislation will recall that until June 3, 1916, pension was payable only when the disability or death was attributable to or due to service or the result of service, or in the line of duty, or caused by service. In Canada the "due to service" principle was entirely discarded in 1916 so far as members of the naval and expeditionary forces on active service were concerned, and a new principle of insurance during service was adopted. At that time this was to apply only to men who were enlisting for service overseas. In 1918 a new element was introduced into the question by an order in council which made members of the permanent force and militia units on pay in Canada part of the Canadian expeditionary force and as such entitled to the benefits of the insurance principle.
The parliamentary committee of 1919 reached the following decisions:	that the
insurance principle applied to all the members of the Canadian forces during service; that as soon as the members of the forces were discharged the "due to service" principle would apply; that the "due to service" principle should apply to members of the forces

Pension Act
who took up occupations during leave; and they decided that after the declaration of peace the "due to service" principle should apply to all members of the forces. They decided that the insurance principle should apply during treatment with the Department of Soldiers' Civil Reestablishment which followed immediately after discharge. For service in a theatre of actual war the insurance principle applied to disabilities which might already have existed previous to service.

subtopic: APPLICATION TO CERTAIN MEMBERS OF CANADIAN AND UNITED KINGDOM FORCES-CHANGES IN PRINCIPLE AND PROCEDURE
speechtext: Did that include venereal disease at that time?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: APPLICATION TO CERTAIN MEMBERS OF CANADIAN AND UNITED KINGDOM FORCES-CHANGES IN PRINCIPLE AND PROCEDURE
speechtext:
Only in relation to those who died on service, I am informed. In 1920 there was another departure. All pensions awarded thereafter were limited to disability or death directly attributable to service. In 1922 we had the basis of the whole insurance principle, section 11; the principle was restored with reference to former members of the expeditionary force who had served in a theatre of actual war if they could show that at the time of discharge from the forces they were suffering from disability, such disability being deemed to have been incurred on or attributable to service, unless the commission established to the contrary. Then in 1923 the final disposition was made. The Ralston commission of that time w'ent thoroughly into this whole principle; strong representations were made to the parliamentary committee of that year that the insurance principle should be restored in respect of all former members of the Canadian expeditionary force, and this was made retroactive to September 1, 1919.
I give this brief historical review, and also the history of the orders in council and the provisions of bill 17 as it was introduced into this house, in order that hon. members may be familiar with the development of the insurance principle in Canada.

subtopic: APPLICATION TO CERTAIN MEMBERS OF CANADIAN AND UNITED KINGDOM FORCES-CHANGES IN PRINCIPLE AND PROCEDURE
speechtext:
Just to
clarify matters, and for the benefit of those of us who are laymen in regard to pension legislation, would the minister give a definition of what he termed the absolute insurance principle? I thought I caught it as he went along, but I should like to be sure about it.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: APPLICATION TO CERTAIN MEMBERS OF CANADIAN AND UNITED KINGDOM FORCES-CHANGES IN PRINCIPLE AND PROCEDURE
speechtext:
It means, Mr. Chairman, that a soldier is protected in respect of anything that may happen to him during service, except in cases of misconduct. That is a very broad definition of the insurance principle.
The select committee appointed by this house gave careful consideration to this question. In that committee, frankly speaking, the opinion was expressed that the
insurance principle should apply to all those serving in Canada. There was another school of thought which held that this would be far too broad and too drastic a departure with so many in sedentary occupations throughout Canada with little prospect of engaging in active service in a theatre of actual war. They were of the opinion that the insurance principle should not apply to all those who were serving in Canada, but that it should absolutely and automatically apply to all those who were in a theatre of actual war.
In regard to this latter term my hon. friend will see, if he looks at the bill originally introduced, that the definition of a theatre of actual war was fairly restricted. That definition has been amended by the committee, after careful consideration, to include service anywhere outside of Canada. That is the first group. In the second place it includes service in any areas or locations in Canada which the governor in council may designate to be theatres of actual war. In the third place it is made to apply to units that may be engaged in active service against hostile forces in any part of Canada; and in the fourth place there-is the all-inclusive reference to contact withe any hostile force within the dominion. So that the definition of a theatre of war as we have-it in this amended bill is by far the broadest, we have ever had in this dominion.
In the committee there was made manifest a laudable desire, which I cannot criticize, that if possible we should apply the insurance principle not only to those who are serving in a theatre of actual war but also to those who are in active training for service in a theatre of war, which, broadly speaking, would apply to certain formations that now may be proceeding, or soon may be proceeding, to a theatre of actual war. We endeavoured, with our legal advisers, as best we could to obtain a line of demarcation to include under the sheltering wing of the insurance principle those who were in active training and who were practically ready to proceed overseas. After consultation with the services themselves the committee found that the line of distinction or demarcation between those who were to have service in Canada and those who were to proceed overseas was not clear. In other words, we found that what appeared to be the desire of the committee, or at least a great section of it, was not a practicable solution. Therefore we came to what might be termed a compromise. It will be found that subsection 3 of section 6 of the present bill introduces what may be termed a new principle in pension legislation in Canada.
Pension Act

subtopic: APPLICATION TO CERTAIN MEMBERS OF CANADIAN AND UNITED KINGDOM FORCES-CHANGES IN PRINCIPLE AND PROCEDURE
speechtext: That is a means test, is it not?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: APPLICATION TO CERTAIN MEMBERS OF CANADIAN AND UNITED KINGDOM FORCES-CHANGES IN PRINCIPLE AND PROCEDURE
speechtext:
Yes. That section, which appears at page 6 of the amended bill, vests in the commission a discretionary power or authority in cases of financial need, where there has been occasioned a serious disability, or where death has ensued, to grant a pension in the discretion of the commission.
At this point I might say that in the old Pension Act there are two sections which confer discretion upon the commission. One is the old section 21, which confers discretion in regard to services of a special and meritorious kind in a theatre of war. But in that case, too, there is an element of need involved, as well as of special meritorious service. Also in section 12, if my memory serves me correctly, discretion is there vested in regard to certain misconduct cases. Again, under section 12, there is the qualification respecting need. But this present section is much broader in its implications and in its significance than either section 21 or section 12. It is frankly designed to meet certain cases of hardship and distress which were brought to the attention of your select committee. Those were cases in which the insurance principle did not apply. The persons concerned could not qualify under the strict letter of the order In council of May 21, 1940, containing the /expression "directly attributable to service as :such"; and therefore in several cases definite hardships ensued.
Your committee endeavoured to meet that situation by placing this discretionary authority in the hands of the Canadian pensions commission. I admit at once it is a very wide power to give to any commission, and unless the committee had an unanimous and complete confidence in the exercise of good judgment on the part of the present commission when using discretionary authorities and powers, I doubt if it would have gone as far as it did.

subtopic: APPLICATION TO CERTAIN MEMBERS OF CANADIAN AND UNITED KINGDOM FORCES-CHANGES IN PRINCIPLE AND PROCEDURE
speechtext: No, sir.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: APPLICATION TO CERTAIN MEMBERS OF CANADIAN AND UNITED KINGDOM FORCES-CHANGES IN PRINCIPLE AND PROCEDURE
speechtext:
I now come to what I might call the date line provisions of the bill. There are three of them. The first date line provision deals with the time of application for pension. In a previous year the date line was made 1936 for those with service in Canada, 1942 for those with service overseas in the great war and, in bill 17 as introduced, there was a date line for the present war. Your committee struck out the 1942 limitation and decided that at least for the present there should be no date set for the present war. So that only the 1936 date line remains in the amended bill.

The second date line provision is concerned with widows. I believe in what I am about to say I am stating fairly well the opinion of the committee, although strong representations were made to us to extend that date to the present time, and not necessarily make it retroactive. The committee did not feel so strongly about the 1930 date line as it did with regard to the 1933 date line, having to do with children's allowances. Strong arguments were placed before the committee to extend the 1933 date line, and equally strong arguments for that extension were put forward by members of the committee themselves. It is felt, however, that this is scarcely the time to alter the principle involved. It has been before the house on several earlier occasions. The leader of the opposition will recall how the date line was established in 1933. As a result of a conference between the then minister of finance, Hon. Mr. Rhodes, and those who were representing all veteran organizations in Canada, an agreement was reached to the effect that allowances be not paid after May 1, 1933. The matter was taken up in this chamber on several occasions subsequent to 1933, but parliament has not varied the provision. I for one feel that with the tremendous obligations confronting our people, this is not the time to do what we could not do between 1933 and 1939.
There are other provisions of the bill which have to do with administration. One important section, dealing with Canadians serving with imperial forces, definitely broadens out the provisions of the old act. There is, however, a difficulty. We have indicated a period of four years prior to the war, in an endeavour to protect our boys in the Royal Canadian Air Force who went overseas in 1936, 1937, 1938 and 1939 for a short term of service with the Royal Air Force, and whose intention it was definitely to return to Canada when those four years had expired. So that not only are those who enlisted since the war for service with the Royal Air Force protected under the sheltering provisions of the section I have indicated, but also those who went over for a period of four years prior to the war are in like manner protected.

subtopic: APPLICATION TO CERTAIN MEMBERS OF CANADIAN AND UNITED KINGDOM FORCES-CHANGES IN PRINCIPLE AND PROCEDURE
speechtext: Was that an ordinary term of enlistment?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: APPLICATION TO CERTAIN MEMBERS OF CANADIAN AND UNITED KINGDOM FORCES-CHANGES IN PRINCIPLE AND PROCEDURE
speechtext: No, it was not in every case. I believe, however, it was a general provision in such commissions at that time.

subtopic: APPLICATION TO CERTAIN MEMBERS OF CANADIAN AND UNITED KINGDOM FORCES-CHANGES IN PRINCIPLE AND PROCEDURE
speechtext: Would that provision apply to any service other than the air force?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: APPLICATION TO CERTAIN MEMBERS OF CANADIAN AND UNITED KINGDOM FORCES-CHANGES IN PRINCIPLE AND PROCEDURE
speechtext: Yes, it will.

subtopic: APPLICATION TO CERTAIN MEMBERS OF CANADIAN AND UNITED KINGDOM FORCES-CHANGES IN PRINCIPLE AND PROCEDURE
speechtext:
It applies to all services.

Pension Act

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: APPLICATION TO CERTAIN MEMBERS OF CANADIAN AND UNITED KINGDOM FORCES-CHANGES IN PRINCIPLE AND PROCEDURE
speechtext:
Yes, to all services, and affecting those who were domiciled in Canada for four years prior to the outbreak of war.
Hon. members will realize that under the agreement we entered into with the British government in connection with the British commonwealth air training plan, pensions for Canadians serving or fighting in England or in Europe are payable by the British authorities. The provisions of this amending bill will supplement such pensions to the Canadian standard. There are, however, benefits in our Pension Act which are not contained in the pension act of Great Britain. The complaint might very well be voiced, and with justice, that we are not making provision to extend these additional benefits in every case. We simply cannot. We cannot do it by legislation. The basis of entitlement is in many cases different in the old country from what it is in Canada, and the benefits consequent upon such basis may not accrue to the men affected, as it would if they were pensioned on a definite Canadian basis. So that the only solution I can see at this time is arrived at not by legislation, but by entering into negotiations with the British ministry of pensions to see if we cannot work out administrative machinery which will give our men all the equality, all the justice and all the fairness to which they are justly entitled.
Perhaps I might take a few minutes to turn to the minor sections of the bill. One of them improves the provisions of the old section 21. Another section extends to children the benefits previously extended to widows under the fifty per cent disability clause. Then there are certain minor sections dealing with matters of administration.
In conclusion I wish to express to the members who sat on the select committee the sincere thanks of the government for the laborious and painstaking attention they paid to every clause in the bill. As an hon. member has said, pension legislation is always difficult. Two great principles are involved: first, that of basic fairness to state and country, and second, justice to those who are serving in this war and those who served in the former war. I think the committee has conscientiously endeavoured to carry out its duty with regard to these two principles. The bill now before us is the result of their deliberations.

subtopic: APPLICATION TO CERTAIN MEMBERS OF CANADIAN AND UNITED KINGDOM FORCES-CHANGES IN PRINCIPLE AND PROCEDURE
speechtext:
The Canadian Pension Act is the magna charta of our fighting forces, the men of our navy, of our army and of our air force, and it is also the magna charta of their wives, their children and their dependent parents. In short, it may be described as the protection of that group of Canadians
who in this war, without doubt, are making the greatest sacrifices and perhaps of those who in the last war did likewise. In this war at any rate they are all doing so of their own free will. For these reasons, if for no others, I suggest it is of the greatest importance that these amendments to the Pension Act should be given the most careful consideration and that the members who are here to-day should suggest improvements thereto whenever they think that such improvements can be made.
Bill No. 17, this bill, amending the Pension Act, as it was brought into the house some weeks ago was very restrictive, far more so than it should have been. For example, it made it quite difficult for a man serving in Canada to qualify for pension-almost impossible, unless he was accidentally shot while on the rifle range, or was knocked over while drilling or otherwise directly engaged in his military training. Except in such cases it would have been almost impossible for him to get a pension or for his dependents to qualify. That applied particularly to cases of disease.
Also the bill as it was brought down contained deadlines which were very restrictive. For instance, the new soldier, the new sailor, the new airman could not apply for a pension unless he applied within seven years of his discharge. That was bringing into the Canadian act for the first time the principle which applies in Great Britain. Again the additional pension payable for the child of a pensioner could not be obtained, so far as the present war is concerned,	unless	that child	wereborn within ten years of the termination of the war.	In other	words,	a married	manreturning	from the	present war, and	laterhaving children, could not get an allowance for any	of them	unless	they were	born
within ten years of the date of the termination of the war. The similar restriction which applies now to men of the old war went into effect in May, 1933, which was fifteen years after the end of that war, and of course we have always contended-some of us at least have done so-that there should be no such restriction with regard to children.
Then the additional pension payable for the wife of a man serving in the present forces was payable under the terms of the bill only if he was married within ten years after the war. In other words, if he married more than ten years after the termination of the war he could not get the allowance for her. Finally, the widow of a man serving in the present forces could get a pension only on his death, no matter whether she was otherwise able to qualify for it or not, if she had married him before he obtained the pension. In other words, if a man came back from the
Pension Act

war, was granted a pension and then married, his widow could not get a pension upon his death, under the provisions of the bill as it was introduced into the house.
Furthermore, the bill contained no relief for a returned soldier of the last war in respect of the various deadlines. As the minister has said, the bill as introduced contained that portion of the Pension Act which stipulated that the man who served overseas in the last war must apply before January 1, 1942, or, if later, only with special leave from the pension commission; also the provision that he received no payment in respect of his wife and children, if the children were born or the wife married after May 1, 1933, and that his widow could not receive a pension if she was married after January 1, 1930. All these deadlines were retained in the bill as it was introduced, although throughout the years we had been complaining, and complaining strongly, that they should be taken out of the act.
Another restriction imposed by the bill as originally presented was that the appeal board, which is the final board in the hearing of an application for pension at the present time, should be reduced from three men to two, and that if there was disagreement between these two the decision would be left to a third man appointed in Ottawa, who had never even heard the witnesses or seen the man. He sat in Ottawa and read the file and based his decision upon the documents. This was a retrograde step that should never have been introduced into the bill.
1 agree with the minister that the committee have worked very hard and have had interesting sessions. In committee some of these restrictions were removed and others were not, and I think it is fair to say that the special committee have made changes, in fact that the bill's own mother, which in this case I suppose would be the minister of pensions, would hardly recognize the child as it comes back to the house.
For example, some of the deadlines have been removed. A man applying for pension, a returned soldier of the last war who served overseas, now has no deadline. He can apply at any time, not being limited to January 1, 1942. Further, there is no deadline for the man serving in the present forces.

speechtext: I understand that there is no deadline now for the returned soldier of the last war in regard to his claim for a pension. subtopic: APPLICATION TO CERTAIN MEMBERS OF CANADIAN AND UNITED KINGDOM FORCES-CHANGES IN PRINCIPLE AND PROCEDURE
speechtext:
Oh, yes. It is fundamental. The man must always show that his disability arose as a result of his service. He must trace it right back to his service in the war. That still stands. The deadline has been removed in the case of the man who served overseas as distinguished from the man who served in Canada only who some years ago was prevented from applying after July 1, 1936. For the man who served overseas, the deadline which was set at January 1, 1942, has now been taken out. As regards the child and wife of a man serving in the new forces, deadlines have been removed, which I think is a very good thing. In other words, no matter when a child may be born, payment can be received in respect of that child. But the deadline still stands with reference to the child and wife of a man who served in the last war.
As regards the widow of a member of the present forces the provision will be found in section 17 of the bill. She can now receive a pension if she married a pensioner within a year of his death, or if she was married to him less than a year before he died, in the event that the board decide that it was not to be expected that he would die within a year. In other words, this provides against death-bed marriages, and I think the committee were agreed that death-bed marriages should not be recognized. But the widow of a man who served in the last war is still subject to the old deadline. Unless she married before January 1, 1930, or before he received his pension, she is just out of luck; she cannot qualify for a pension.
The committee wiped out the provision that the appeal board membership should be cut from three to two; they insisted that the board remain as it was, composed of three members. They made another change in section 6 of the bill, which affects section 11, subsection 1, paragraph (c) of the act, by striking out the words "or was a congenital defect". As the act stood formerly, the meaning of these words was that no pension could be paid where the disease or disability was a congenital defect. That aroused great antagonism in nervous and mental cases. Apparently a portion of the medical fraternity had decided that if a man became a nervous wreck or perhaps went out of his mind subsequent to the war, it was because he was born to do so; that he had a congenital defect and that his war service had nothing to do with the disability. Such a ruling never seemed reasonable to the lay members of the house, and the doctors who served with us on

Pension Act
the committee this year agreed with us and recommended that these words should be deleted.
Another important change is to be found at the top of page 3 of the bill. Subsection 9 of section 3 of the act is amended to provide that the chairman of the pension commission shall have the status of a deputy minister. He had this status before 1936, but in that year was deprived of such standing and made subject to the deputy minister of pensions and national health. In order that the pension commission may be more independent it has been decided that the chairman should be given the status of a deputy minister.
The minister has referred already to section 20 of the bill, which introduces a new section of the act to be known as section 46A. This provides that Canadians who serve with the imperial forces will be entitled to have the difference between their imperial pension and a Canadian, pension made up by the Canadian government. This is of vital importance to the men training under the commonwealth air training scheme. It may perhaps surprise hon. members of the committee to know that all Canadians who train under that scheme become imperial airmen once they leave the shores of Canada; they are paid by the British government and receive their pensions from the British government, pursuant to the agreement between Great Britain, Canada, Australia and New Zealand. It was of the greatest importance, therefore, that these men should be able to get the same rates of pension as those who serve in the Canadian air force.
In this connection there is one thing I should like the minister to explain more fully.
I should like to know what he is prepared to do in order, for example, to permit a Canadian airman serving under the commonwealth training plan to establish in Canada his right to a pension rather than in Great Britain. Is it not possible for us to arrange with the British government to send, to Canada a pensions representative who would have the authority to decide whether or not a Canadian airman serving under the commonwealth air training plan is entitled to a pension, rather than require the airman to fight his case in England?
There still remain certain serious defects in this bill, which will also be defects in the act. A good example will be found in section 1, the definitions section. The definition of "member of the forces" does not include men who serve in the auxiliary forces. For example, a Salvation Army man, a Y.M.C.A. man or a Canadian Legion man may be serving overseas with the troops. For all purposes he is treated as a member of the forces except when it comes to pension. If
he is disabled or killed a pension can be granted only by order in council. I submit that that should not be necessary. A Canadian Legion man was drowned a couple of weeks ago along with some of our troops on his way to Great Britain. The widow of that man will be able to obtain a pension only by order in council. I submit that all such cases should be covered by the act.

speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman go as far as to include C.P.S. members?

speechtext: Civil protection services.

subtopic: APPLICATION TO CERTAIN MEMBERS OF CANADIAN AND UNITED KINGDOM FORCES-CHANGES IN PRINCIPLE AND PROCEDURE
speechtext:
In some provinces they are called A.R.P. men. They certainly should be protected, whether under this act or some other I do not know. Their rights should be clearly defined by dominion statute.
There is another more serious defect in this measure. It still will be far too difficult, even with the amendments provided by this bill, for a man to qualify for pension. After the last war a man qualified for pension whether he had served in England, in France or in Canada, under section 11, subsection 1, paragraph (a) of the act. The keywords of the whole Pension Act were to be found there, as follows:
-was attributable to or was incurred during such military service.
This was the "incurred on" principle, sometimes known as the insurance principle. It applied to all men who served in the last war, whether their service was overseas or in Canada. Another relevant provision was subsection 2 of section 11 of the act. It is described in the marginal note as covering post-war disabilities. In other words, a provision is put into the Pension Act to cover men serving in peace time. They or their dependents can get pensions only if the disabilities are attributable to military service as such. The words "as such" are very restrictive. As I say, this provision applied to men serving in peace time.
About the time the present war broke out- in fact, on September 2, 1939, just before the declaration of war-the government provided by order in council that the "incurred-on" principle-in other words the insurance principle-should apply to all men serving in the Canadian active service force, whether in England, in Canada, in Iceland, the West Indies, or elsewhere. All men in the Canadian active service force were protected by the insurance principle by that order in council, and it stayed in effect until May 21, 1940,

subtopic: APPLICATION TO CERTAIN MEMBERS OF CANADIAN AND UNITED KINGDOM FORCES-CHANGES IN PRINCIPLE AND PROCEDURE
speechtext: Is that changed now in the bill?

subtopic: APPLICATION TO CERTAIN MEMBERS OF CANADIAN AND UNITED KINGDOM FORCES-CHANGES IN PRINCIPLE AND PROCEDURE
speechtext:
I am coming to that in just a minute. I think the house should lay it down as a principle, without equivocation, that the man in the active army, in the navy or in the air force who is going overseas, and who is merely here in the meantime training for that purpose-in other words, the man who is on "active service" as the Canadian people understand it, the man who is really going to do the fighting-should have the protection of the "incurred-on" principle, whether up to the time of the accident he had been able to get out of Canada or not.
In other words, the men of the third Canadian division now in Canada waiting to go overseas, the men of the armoured division, the men of the tank brigade, the men of the fourth Canadian division, all on active service and all ready to go and do the fighting, should be protected, even though they have not yet been able to proceed overseas.
In spite of these considerations, however, the committee bring in a half-and-half recommendation on a question about which there 
should be no compromise. What a majority of the committee has done is to bring in, as embodied in the new section 11, subsection 2, a provision extending the peace-time principle a little by changing the words "attributable to military service as such" to "disability which arose out of or was directly connected with such military service." It is still very much restricted. I doubt whether it will cover cases such as I mentioned a few minutes ago, of men killed while returning from leave, or dying as the result of an epidemic of disease while in barracks.
Then, to go further and cover a few borderline cases of hardship, the committee inserts subsection 3 of section 11, which provides that where there is a serious disability-it must be serious-or death-that is the first restriction -and, where the man or his dependents are in necessitous circumstances-that is the second restriction-the commission may, if they see fit-for the whole thing is left to the discretion of the pension commission- award a pension, not exceeding the amount that the man would get if he were overseas. It may be considerably less, but they have power to go up to that amount, as well as to pay a lower amount.
I will add no more to my statement with regard to this defect, except to repeat that it is a serious one, and that the men who are going overseas to do the fighting for this country are entitled to the protection of the "incurred-on" principle.
A third defect, which also is serious, is that the children and the wives of the men of the old army are not protected, if the child was born, or if the woman was married, after May 1, 1933. No matter what deal was made here in that year-and there is some question as to what it was-I have never been able to see the fairness of saying to a man with, say, three children, one born before and two born after the first of May, 1933: "We will give you the allowance for your one child, but we will not give you the allowance for the other two"; or to say to the young veteran of the last war, the man who enlisted at the age of sixteen or seventeen and did not get married until a few years ago, "The child of an older soldier can get the allowance, but there is no allowance for your child". Such an unfair discrimination should have no place on the statute books of Canada. These men should be encouraged to have children rather than the contrary.
Of the sections of the bill which apply, sections 13 and 22 have to do with the wife and children, and sections 16 and 17 have to do with the widow. So far as widows of the men of the last war are concerned, they are still not entitled to pension unless they were

Pension Act
married before the husband got his pension or before January 1, 1930. The Canadian Legion suggested that the date be changed to January 1, 1940, but that was not accepted.
Finally, I wish to point out to the committee something which is not, strictly speaking, a defect of the Pension Act: that it is impossible now to make any change this session in the War Veterans Allowance Act. It was decided that some provision for widows who were not otherwise pensionable could best be made in the War Veterans Allowance Act. This group of widows made out a good case, but apparently the only way in which they can be covered is under the War Veterans Allowance Act.

subtopic: APPLICATION TO CERTAIN MEMBERS OF CANADIAN AND UNITED KINGDOM FORCES-CHANGES IN PRINCIPLE AND PROCEDURE
speechtext: Will the War Veterans Allowance Act be amended this session to take care of that?

subtopic: APPLICATION TO CERTAIN MEMBERS OF CANADIAN AND UNITED KINGDOM FORCES-CHANGES IN PRINCIPLE AND PROCEDURE
speechtext: No; as I have said, the act is not to be amended at this session, which means that no protection will be given at this time to this deserving class. It means also that relief cannot be afforded to the men of the old imperial army who have been in Canada for a period of years and who are claiming some benefit from the War Veterans Allowance Act. It also means that there will be no amendment for the benefit of veterans of the Riel rebellion.

subtopic: APPLICATION TO CERTAIN MEMBERS OF CANADIAN AND UNITED KINGDOM FORCES-CHANGES IN PRINCIPLE AND PROCEDURE
speechtext: That is pretty hard on the widows of the war veterans.

subtopic: APPLICATION TO CERTAIN MEMBERS OF CANADIAN AND UNITED KINGDOM FORCES-CHANGES IN PRINCIPLE AND PROCEDURE
speechtext: That sums up my complaints and my suggestions in connection with this bill. I believe the bill should be most carefully considered by the house and that they should insist that the proper changes be made. I am certain that the Canadian people, if they could all be here, would wish us to go the limit to protect the men who are going to do our fighting, and their dependents.

subtopic: APPLICATION TO CERTAIN MEMBERS OF CANADIAN AND UNITED KINGDOM FORCES-CHANGES IN PRINCIPLE AND PROCEDURE
speechtext:
A returned soldier of the last great war who enlisted in the present war was on his way overseas but fell ill of pneumonia on the Atlantic shore and was returned home. Would he be entitled under the present bill to receive a pension? The man to whom I refer is a married man with many children, and actually starving. I tried to obtain something for him from the pension board, but was told he was not entitled to pension because he was bound to prove that the disease which led to his discharge was attributable to war service. To me that seems absolutely unjust. I should be very glad if the new legislation in its letter and spirit would cover such cases.
The hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) mentioned that during the last war the Pension Act covered not only those
who went to France but also those who were in England. I know many instances in which, so far as the civil service commission's regulations are concerned, a distinction is made between a returned soldier who served in France and one who remained in England; to those who went only as far as England they refused the advantages given to those who served in France. I think the department of pensions must have something to do with that because they have a representative on the civil service commission.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: APPLICATION TO CERTAIN MEMBERS OF CANADIAN AND UNITED KINGDOM FORCES-CHANGES IN PRINCIPLE AND PROCEDURE
speechtext:
With regard to the last point, there would be a preference to men who saw service in France in the last war over those who remained in England, unless the latter had a disability pension.
With regard to the pneumonia case, under the terms of the order in council of May 21, 1940, the man would be pensionable only if his illness was directly due to service as such. Under the broadened provision of the present legislation it might be pensionable under subsections 2 and 3 of section 6. If this measure passes my hon. friend should reapply in regard to that case.

subtopic: APPLICATION TO CERTAIN MEMBERS OF CANADIAN AND UNITED KINGDOM FORCES-CHANGES IN PRINCIPLE AND PROCEDURE
speechtext:
The hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) made a splendid survey of this bill as we have it before us in its amended form. As a member of the committee which spent considerable time discussing this bill I should like first to compliment the chairman of the committee, who did a fine job. I might add that the members of the committee were fairly harmonious in their deliberations. Some of us may not have obtained all that we would like in the way of amendments, despite the fact that the bill in its present form is scarcely recognizable as the one with which the committee started.
The application of the insurance principle might have been a little broader. True the provision as to necessitous circumstances does give broad authority to the pension commission, but, like the hon. member for Vancouver South, I think all who are training and are in category A to go overseas should have the
Pension Act

insurance principle broadly applied to them. It should not be considered a matter of charity or necessitous circumstances. I believe we could have taken care of these people on a much broader basis than we have. We cannot estimate in dollars and cents what we owe to those men who are going to be a decisive factor in this war, which is being fought in order that we may in future enjoy our way of life. We should be very considerate of those people who make such tremendous sacrifices, and their dependents.
Coming to the matter of the deadline, we made some headway when the deadline was withdrawn for those serving in the present war. I feel very strongly that children bom after May 1, 1933, should not be discriminated against. It is also a discrimination against the younger soldiers. A man who went to the great war in his 'teens found economic conditions most difficult following the war. There was the man of the right type who, having met the girl who he thought would be his helpmate and would make a fine mother for his family, felt that he could not afford to marry for many years following the great war, and that I think is to his credit. Many of the men who viewed the economic affairs of this country in this light are to-day among our better citizens, and certainly their offspring are of a type that we should be fostering in this country to-day. I do not think there is any trouble about disunity, and so on, among these men who have rendered service, and to their offspring this country owes some obligation. Therefore I feel rather keenly as to the deadline, and not only as respects the widow married after January 1, 1930; I think we might have taken away that deadline with respect to those children. It is unfair discrimination not only against the children but against the father, who may have been a younger soldier and for the best reasons in the world did not marry until later in life.
The compassionate pension or supplementary award referred to on page 8 is a step in the right direction. Widows now are granted pension if married a year prior to the granting of pension, or if the commission is satisfied that the husband had every prospect of living at least a year. That is another step in the right direction.
I should like to urge further, as did the previous speaker, that we make an effort to have a representative of the British government stationed in this country; if we did so we might obtain much more for the men who are taking part in the commonwealth air training plan. A great deal more might be accomplished in that regard.

There are two or three clauses that I intend to discuss as we come to them. I am extremely sorry, especially on behalf of the widows, that we are not going to have the War Veterans Allowance Act amended at this session. Many of those widows are entitled to further consideration as soon as possible. It has been pointed out that they will not receive any consideration unless that act is also amended; and the veterans of the Riel rebellion, who probably are in necessitous circumstances at this time, cannot be provided for either. I trust that the government, at the earliest possible day, will amend the War Veterans Allowance Act to deal with these matters.

It is
perhaps a harsh thing to ask for, but I should like the Canadian people to know just what additional financial burden this bill will impose. We may as well face the facts. I am not opposing any such additional burden, but I think we should know what the increased money liability is likely to be as a result of this bill. I think we ought to know.

subtopic: APPLICATION TO CERTAIN MEMBERS OF CANADIAN AND UNITED KINGDOM FORCES-CHANGES IN PRINCIPLE AND PROCEDURE
speechtext: Well, Mr. Chairman, I fear it is impossible even to forecast what the financial obligations may be. I do not know that anyone could do that, because naturally, in the first place, it would depend upon the provisions of the legislation, which to-day is being broadened as compared to what it has been up to the present time, except for the first few months of the war. In the second place it would definitely depend upon the numbers of casualties or disabilities with which the forces might be confronted. For the first seven months of the war the amount of pensions awarded was very small,-only $5,176.43. For the first twelve months the figure was $188,522.43, making a total of $193,698.86. That, of course, was under the provisions of the orders in council.

appreciate that possibly no one could give any definite data with respect to the pension liability that may result from this war. But could not the commission give an estimate in regard to the increased obligation resulting from the greater benefits to those who served in the last war and their dependents? Could they not make a distinction between the two wars?

It is not my intention to [DOT]detain the committee at any great length, Rut having listened with considerable interest to the explanation given by the minister I have come to the conclusion-and I hope the minister will correct me if I am in error- that the men of the third division now serving in Canada, preparing for whatever may lie ahead, are definitely uncertain as to whether they may receive pensions if they become disabled, except under certain circumstances and -at the will of persons who have been given authority to deal with these matters. That,
I gather, is the gist of what has been said by the minister. I am not criticizing the committee, which I think did a splendid job-

speechtext: Perhaps my hon. friend would prefer that I wait until he is through, but there is one provision in the present bill which I forgot to mention. If anyone goes to a theatre of war and then returns to Canada, the insurance principle applies to him for all time. *Once the men go overseas from Canada they are completely protected.

subtopic: APPLICATION TO CERTAIN MEMBERS OF CANADIAN AND UNITED KINGDOM FORCES-CHANGES IN PRINCIPLE AND PROCEDURE
speechtext:
I am not concerned with the man who goes overseas and then returns to Canada. My remarks have to do with the great army of men who have volunteered, particularly at this time when further volunteers are being sought by the thousands. These men cannot feel any sense of security, with relation to pensions for their wives, if they go overseas within the next few months. That is the only criticism I have to offer; and I do so advisedly. A great many of the men now in the army, the air force and the navy- though I have particular reference to the army-have younger brothers twenty-one or twenty-two years of age who are now being [DOT]enrolled in the defence forces, in a sense under compulsion. There have been a number of serious accidents, many of which I could mention ; these accidents are bound to continue, and any man in the active army to-day, serving at some training centre, learning of the action that has been taken by this government, will find himself in a very difficult and uncertain position when he comes to discuss the matter with his younger brothers who are soon to follow in his footsteps.
I point this out to the minister because from my own experience I know what effect this bill, and the other statutes that will follow, will have on the minds of many men now serving with the active forces. I am
receiving letters every day in regard to this matter, as I am sure other hon. members are; within a short time these men may be leaving for Egypt, Africa or some other distant points, but in the meantime serious accidents are happening almost every day. The other day at Petawawa a man lost his life in an accident which occurred through no fault of his own; yet under these provisions the families of these men are to a great extent debarred from any possibility of gaining security in the days to come. Now, when recruits are being sought in goodly numbers, is the best time to give this matter consideration and to see to it that these men shall not have to go overseas in the days to come with this feeling of insecurity in their hearts as a result of the actions of this committee and of the government.

subtopic: APPLICATION TO CERTAIN MEMBERS OF CANADIAN AND UNITED KINGDOM FORCES-CHANGES IN PRINCIPLE AND PROCEDURE
speechtext: I have just one or two questions to ask the minister. How many men have been discharged, after service, since the outbreak of war; how many who have served overseas have been returned to Canada; how many serving in Canada have been discharged; of all these, how many are in receipt of pension? I agree with the last speaker that if ever there was a time when the morale of this nation should be upheld and when everything should be done to cause those going into the armed forces and their dependents to realize that their service will not be forgotten and that in the event of sacrifice it will be properly rewarded, that time is now. Subsection 2 of the new section 11 amounts to this, as I understand it, that if a man is killed while in service in Canada, or while going on or returning from leave, or accidentally while in camp as the result of negligence, we will say, on the part of someone driving a motor vehicle not connected with the military forces, he would not be entitled to pension.

The minister was
very careful to say that that does not necessarily follow now. The amendment provides that pension shall be payable where death or injuiy "arose out of or was directly connected with such military service." I am reminded that under the Workmen's Compensation Act the words "arose out of" have been interpreted time without number. The interpretation is generally to the effect that a person must actually have been engaged in the work at the time the injury was received or occurred, within the scope of the employment.
The minister has indicated that under circumstances such as those to which I have
Pension Act

referred, a person would not necessarily be disqualified. Will he tell the committee that if under such circumstances a person is killed or injured, under the section as amended such person's relatives or such person himself would be entitled to pension? I am sure he would not go that far. Well, if we want to get recruits we shall have to extend to those serving in Canada to-day a right of pension similar to that enjoyed by those who served in England in the last war.
Subsection 3 provides that where a pension is not awardable, the pensions commission may, under certain circumstances, grant a pension.

ex gratia.

subtopic: APPLICATION TO CERTAIN MEMBERS OF CANADIAN AND UNITED KINGDOM FORCES-CHANGES IN PRINCIPLE AND PROCEDURE

Yes. Either a
person is or is not entitled to pension, and I protest against placing under the control of any commission, however commendable it may be, the power to make a decision awarding or refusing to award a pension beyond the qualifications stipulated in the statute. Let us amend this measure so that the men to whom the last speaker referred may, while serving their country, receive a pension. To-day on every hand we read about the deaths of men on service in Canada. The dependents of those men should be entitled to pension.
It is intended under the suggested amendments to allow the commission to give such persons pensions if they decide so to do. Let us make it definite enough so that such persons will not have to depend upon the interpretation of words as restrictive as "arose out of" or "was directly connected with such military service."

I refer to the number of widows who are in the twelve to twenty class and the amount of money that would be required to give them pensions. I believe I brought this matter up once before.
With regard to the insurance principle of the bill, that is, for those men who are really in the active service forces, it must be remembered that as matters stand now it is more in the nature of workmen's compensation. Under workmen's compensation, the workman of the country has an opportunity to obtain accident and sickness insurance which will take care of him while he is off his job; but conditions to-day make it impossible for a man in the armed forces to get sickness or accident insurance to protect him in any way against such unforeseen occurrences as motor accidents, or sickness when he is, so to speak, off his job. I think, therefore, the government should do something to meet that situation. It is most unfair that a man who is thrifty, a man who has a family and wishes to visit his home, should be exposed to the dangers of hitch-hiking, because, under present circumstances, if he goes by rail he has to pay his own railway fare and consequently he is forced to hitch-hike. We know that accidents occur in hitch-hiking, and should one of these men meet with an accident he is out of luck. Something should be done about the matter. I agree with the hon. member for Vancouver South that, for the active service forces, those men who will go overseas, we should see to it that they are protected against accident and sickness when they are on leave or are not on duty.
Another matter which I have in mind is with reference to the auxiliary forces, those men who go over with the Y.M.C.A., and so forth. Such men are doing as fine a job as the other fellows, and the charitable institutions will not take care of them in any way.
Pension Act

They have practically the same status as the soldier, and I suggest that something might be done to have them made members of the forces so that they would be able to qualify for pensions.
I have always thought it was a hardship on children born after 1933 to be unpensionable. Many a young fellow went to the last war at an early age and, after coming back, found it almost impossible for many years to get a job, and it was only when he was getting on a little better later on in life that he decided to get married. If his family were born after 1933 the children are deprived of benefits, if he is pensionable. That defect should be remedied. It would not cost the country very much.
The same remark applies to the woman who got married after 1930. There was a good reason for putting that provision in the bill originally. I believe it was called the gold-diggers clause. The object was to prevent the sort of thing implied in the term, but that has gone by the board now. Any woman who married a man after 1930 did so because she was pretty fond of him. She took care of him, certainly devoted a good deal of her time to his welfare and probably made a great sacrifice herself. That is another feature which should be improved.
I cannot speak too strongly on the question of the insurance principle with regard to this bill. Some provision should be made to take care of men from this point of view.

subtopic: APPLICATION TO CERTAIN MEMBERS OF CANADIAN AND UNITED KINGDOM FORCES-CHANGES IN PRINCIPLE AND PROCEDURE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, first. I want to join with the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross) in complimenting the chairman of the pensions committee, of which I am a member, upon the manner in which he handled a most difficult job. I think he made a good job of it.
Second, I should like to make a few observations with respect to the manner in which the committee itself handled its work. This is the first time that I have served upon a pensions committee and I had some apprehension that the committee might adopt a partisan attitude because government members dominated the membership. I am naturally suspicious. I wa$ however, agreeably surprised to find that partisan politics were completely forgotten and that the problems relating to men who are serving in this war and who served in the last war were considered on the basis of merit alone. I think every member of the committee was fully conscious of his duty with respect to those problems and had no thought of politics or anything like that.
The hon. member for Vancouver South has given a thorough analysis of the bill as it stands at the present time. I agree with practically everything he has said, but there are some things which I view in a different light. I believe this bill will overcome many features which were objectionable in the first draft. It has relieved my mind with respect to certain sections in the act and the way in which they were administered. The real test of any legislation is its administration. In my opinion we shall get out of this bill just what the people who have the responsibility of administering it are ready to give us. All the departmental representatives who have to do with the administration of pensions sat in

Pension Act
on that committee. They heard its deliberations, and I think they understand what was in the minds of the men who gave them their instructions for the final drafting of this bill. After listening to those men, I am reasonably certain that many of the problems which faced the old soldier in the past will be lightened to a considerable extent.
I am disappointed to find out that no changes will be made in the War Veterans' Allowance Act at this session. I allowed some of the sections in this bill to pass without objection because I understood that certain sections of the other act would be amended and that certain classes of pensioners or people would be taken care of under that act. I refer particularly to the widows of men who served in a theatre of war and -who no doubt went to premature graves as a result of that service.
I repeat. I am disappointed to find out that these widows are not to be taken care of by an amendment to the War Veterans' Allowance Act. My information was that they would be, and I hope something may still be done because I understand the committee is still functioning.
I am one member of the committee who believes in the full maintenance of the insurance principle. I am convinced that perhaps 50 per cent of the problems of the war veterans are due to the fact that there is no other type of social legislation which will take care of a man who breaks down in industry and becomes prematurely aged. Many of the veterans who have been and are now filing claims are men who should be taken care of by some other form of social legislation. Since, however, we have no legislation to take care of them, they try to relate their problem to the only source of relief they have.
The full maintenance of the insurance principle will help the man being requisitioned for service. I do not think there is a man entering our service, whether for overseas or in Canada, who thinks of himself alone. What bothers 99 per cent of them is what is going to happen to their families. When a man offers to fight for his country, he offers his life, but he wants assurance that his family will be taken care of. That is why I favour the full maintenance of the insurance principle. I have a large group in mind, those industrial workers who have protective insurance, compensation insurance, or other schemes whereby their families are taken care of in the event of their death. When such men are requisitioned for service they must leave their employment, and as a result they lose this protective insurance for their families. I am speaking about the $1.30 a day man. Such a man has not sufficient income
to continue to carry ordinary insurance, and consequently his family is left without any protection.
If something happens to him which cannot be related to service, his family are the real sufferers. The present act takes care of this problem to a large degree, but not to the extent I should like it to do. There is a new section which will take care of the soldier whose disability or death is not related to military service. I am thinking of the man who gets into a tangle not related to his military service and loses his life. If the dependents are found to be in necessitous circumstances, the commission have the discretion to award a pension or to take care of them.

subtopic: APPLICATION TO CERTAIN MEMBERS OF CANADIAN AND UNITED KINGDOM FORCES-CHANGES IN PRINCIPLE AND PROCEDURE
speechtext: No matter what the cause of death may be.

subtopic: APPLICATION TO CERTAIN MEMBERS OF CANADIAN AND UNITED KINGDOM FORCES-CHANGES IN PRINCIPLE AND PROCEDURE
speechtext:
That takes care of the situation to a considerable degree. I repeat, I think the committee did a good job and went a long way toward relieving my mind of many of the matters that had been bothering it.
I should like to see nursing sisters who serve in a theatre of war placed in a category by themselves. I do not think they should be dealt with in the ordinary way, by having to appear before boards and travel the routine pension route. When any one with the delicate mechanism of a woman serves two or three years in England, or in any other theatre of war, she has suffered to such an extent that compensation for her services should be very easy to get. She should not have to undergo the relatively rough routine followed by the average soldier.
I am interested also in the men who are doing convoy work at the present time. There is an order in council that protects men who serve in that capacity.

subtopic: APPLICATION TO CERTAIN MEMBERS OF CANADIAN AND UNITED KINGDOM FORCES-CHANGES IN PRINCIPLE AND PROCEDURE
speechtext: Not being enlisted men.

speechtext:
Yes. That order in council
covers men who serve on ships of Canadian registry, but a large percentage of the ships sailing from Canadian ports are of British, Greek or some foreign registry. If our Canadian boys who are engaged in this very necessary and dangerous service are injured or killed during that service, there is no pension and no protection so far as the Canadian government is concerned; they or their dependents must apply to the British government or the government of registry of the ship. It is a long, hard road to travel. I had to do with one case; it was satisfactorily settled by the British imperial pension authorities here in Ottawa, but it took, as we can well understand, considerable time to adjust.
Pension Act

A special committee dealt with the matter and recommended that it be given consideration. I hope that, before this discussion is concluded, the minister will say something about the question.
There came before the committee another matter, of which I have not heard anything, and I should like to know exactly where we stand. A Mr. Beaton appeared before the committee in behalf of long service pensioners. They have been dealing with the Department of National Defence for a number of years. Their pensions are very, very small, having been fixed years ago in accordance with rates paid at that time. There are not many of these pensioners, but according to the description Mr. Beaton gave the committee, most of them are now objects of charity. I understood, or hoped, that some action would be taken in their behalf.
