subtopic: APPLICATION TO CERTAIN MEMBERS OF CANADIAN AND UNITED KINGDOM FORCES-CHANGES IN PRINCIPLE AND PROCEDURE
speechtext:
Another matter I had in mind-strictly1- speaking it may not relate to the bill, although it has to do with pensions and national health

is treatment for men discharged from the present army. As I understand the situation, between ten and twelve thousand have been discharged for medical reasons. On leaving the army they have made applications, and their claims have been examined by the pensions department. I should like to know-and I raised the question in committee-the exact status of this group as regards hospitalization and treatment. The minister answered this morning that they were entitled to treatment for a year after their discharge. I believe I am safe in saying that 75 per cent of the men who are discharged as medically unfit, and who have a family to maintain, go to their homes. If such a man is taken to hospital and given treatment under the conditions outlined by the minister, he leaves a family at home who have nothing wherewith to maintain themselves while the head of the family is in hospital. I believe that is a matter which should receive more consideration. I hope, however, that these defects will be attended to in the future, either by the house or in the course of the administration of the act, by order in council or otherwise.
Speaking of the work of the pensions committee as I saw it, I believe that it has functioned, not with the purpose of making political capital, but as recognizing the problems and disabilities of those who go into the army to serve us, and trying to care for them and fulfil our obligations to them to as large an extent as we can, consistent with the financial resources of the country. I am not ashamed to say here that I believe the committee has done a very good job, and that this bill will go a long way to relieve many disabilities which were not provided for in the original draft.

subtopic: APPLICATION TO CERTAIN MEMBERS OF CANADIAN AND UNITED KINGDOM FORCES-CHANGES IN PRINCIPLE AND PROCEDURE
speechtext:
I believe that the able minister, the splendid chairman of the committee and all its members deserve the thanks, gratitude and unanimous support of the house

Pension Act
and of the country in the good work which they have done since this session started. I am personally aware of the committee's good work, because I have read every day its proceedings and was a witness before it. I 'have had applications for copies of the minutes from some of the leaders of four of the largest denominations and from prominent citizens in Canada. The committee has given good and efficient service, and is a great credit to the committee system of this house.
Only general principles, constructions and changes of import are dealt with in the bill, because this is in many important features a very different war from the last one.
While the bill and the explanatory notes clearly elucidate the principles and procedure and administration of the measure, there are some amendments which, to my mind, might have been included.
The provision which makes the chairman of the commission a deputy minister is, I think, a good one; it will be useful when parliament is not in session, increasing efficiency and making the act more workable.
Another matter upon which I wish briefly to comment is that of soldier insurance, in connection with life, unemployment and demobilization after the war clauses. The system in effect in the United States resulted in a marked economy in their national pension system, and I was in hopes that the committee, although this may not be the right place to include it-

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: APPLICATION TO CERTAIN MEMBERS OF CANADIAN AND UNITED KINGDOM FORCES-CHANGES IN PRINCIPLE AND PROCEDURE
speechtext: May I interrupt my hon. friend? The question of soldier insurance has yet to be considered by the committee, and doubtless there will be a recommendation with reference to it.

subtopic: APPLICATION TO CERTAIN MEMBERS OF CANADIAN AND UNITED KINGDOM FORCES-CHANGES IN PRINCIPLE AND PROCEDURE
speechtext:
I thank the minister and hope it will come, but I w'as going to remark that I believe a bigger economy in pensions would be possible if we had the matter included in this bill, thus forming part of a coordinated system of direct and indirect legislative aid to the soldier and his family.
I was in hopes that something more would be done to help reestablish the large, body of men who were accepted at the outbreak of war, and after three to six months in the army were discharged as physically unfit. Some additional consideration, it seems to me, should be given to them.
Another point of importance has to do with compensation for the dependents of men who have been killed on the highways or who have died while in attendance at camp. They surely were on military service when killed travelling on leave to and from camp. I should have liked to see some additional provision for them.	.
Another matter is regarding the setting up of the commission chairman as a deputy minister to administer the act, which I think by these amendments will be enhanced and speeded up. I believe the time is coming when, in view of the rising cost of living, we must have a more liberal provision in the Pension Act and a cost of living bonus for our soldiers. Railway employees and civil servants are asking for a cost of living bonus, and the widows and orphans of soldiers are very much handicapped by the present scale. A revision should be had.
Another feature that I think the committee might have taken up further, although they cannot do it all in one bite, is the further education of soldiers' children. The minister has made many changes since this started and should go still further. Regarding hospitalization and the burial of the dead, I hope that with the new system and definitions the minister will have increased powers.
The people of Canada wish to see the soldiers dealt with generously. They have never expected, since the first German war ended and the second started, that we should act as dead-beats to our returned soldiers. The government have done very well in this connection, but more aid is needed, and with the increased powers and a more liberal construction of the new measure I hope the good work will keep up. I believe that these soldiers should very soon have a bonus for the increased cost of living.

subtopic: APPLICATION TO CERTAIN MEMBERS OF CANADIAN AND UNITED KINGDOM FORCES-CHANGES IN PRINCIPLE AND PROCEDURE
speechtext:
Let me first congratulate the chairman and the members of the pensions committee who have made a painstaking study of the problem of pensions and have reached unanimity, which is a real accomplishment. I also congratulate the minister upon the attention that he has given to this problem, and all hon. members who have spoken, and particularly my friends the hon. member for Vancouver South, the hon. member for Souris and the hon. member for Broadview, who has just concluded his little speech.
I agree that all men who have been in a theatre of war should be helped when they have suffered a disability that prevents them from doing the same work as they did before enlistment. If a man enlists, of course he makes a sacrifice, and if he is wounded or becomes disabled, he has reason to expect the state to come to his aid and help him to resume his life in the same condition as if he had not been to war and had not become disabled. That seems a reasonable point of view. There is no necessity for exciting pathos with regard to these cases; there is not
Pension Act

a single member of the committee who does not appreciate the gallantry of our army in all its three branches. I leave it to others who have more oratorical power than I have ever been gifted with to express the feelings in which we all share.
There is, however, one point that seems to have been overlooked with regard to soldiers. It is the necessity of investigation of each case throughout Canada. The reply may be "Oh, it is too expensive". It is not too expensive, because at the present time we are paying about 854.000,000 a year for pensions, ordinary pensions being included. It is a formidable sum, and we do not know w'hat will be the cost of pensions for this war. I sincerely hope that the fewest possible number of those in the forces will be wounded or disabled; that is the wish of every one of us. But whatever happens, we must expect to pay a very heavy bill.
At the present time the amount of 854,000,000 is out of proportion to what the Canadian people can pay. I do not want any deserving case to be overlooked; I do not want any soldier who has been wounded on the battlefield to be refused pension. I state that clearly and positively. On the other hand there are cases in which a man deserves a pension and does not need it. By virtue of the law he has a right to it, but I wonder whether it is not possible in each case to say to him: "Joe, you are entitled to this according to the statutes of this country; no one can deprive you of it; but since you do not need it, do you insist on receiving it?" The answer will be left to him, and whatever answer he makes deserves * respect. He has freedom to decide whether he will draw this pension whether he needs it or not. There are other cases where men have been awarded pensions that they did not deserve, and in those cases the investigator should see to it that the payment of those pensions is stopped at once.
Another class of cases deserving of sympathy is that of those men who have been at the front in a theatre of war for two or three or four years, either on land, at sea or in the air, men who were strong when they enlisted and who still looked strong when they were discharged but who suffered from rheumatism perhaps ten or twenty years before they would if they had not seen this war service. Those men deserve special consideration. I cannot understand how a pension can be refused to a man who has been at the front for two or three years, who has been living like a caveman in the mud of the trenches, in winter as well as in summer; you cannot expect that man to be 100 per cent healthy when he comes out even if he is discharged

as A-l. I have known soldiers who have been at war for three or four years who looked just as husky as any policeman but whose health was not good. They were declared sick by boards of specialists, men of high standing in their profession, but were turned back; they could not get anything.
A case that happened recently was that of a poor fellow who was in the army for a couple of years. I saw him quite often. He was examined by the board of pension commissioners and awarded a pension. He had been at war for two years. He was suffering from rheumatism which at times was very painful. He was awarded a nice pension of $3.75 a month; and he has a wife and some children. I found it really shocking. At the time I thanked the pension commission; when I was told that a cheqtie for S47 was being issued, I thought the man was to receive a pension of $47 a month. But this cheque covered only the arrears for a certain length of time, and he was told officially that he would receive only 83.75 a month. How can a man live on twelve or thirteen cents a day? It is absurd.
I am not in favour of imposing an undue burden on the treasury, but it seems to me it is time we made a check of this matter. At present all we know is the total amount paid for pensions, but I am sure that if we had an honest investigation by independent men, with power to decide each case on its merits and without regard to party considerations, the pension bill could be cut by at least a third. Then the country would have to pay only two-thirds of the 854,000,000 or 855,000,000 that is being paid now. That is worth considering because, if-and God forbid-more of our boys become disabled, the country will have to look after them, and we shall have to find the money somehow. It seems to me the best way to do that would be to check over w'hat we are paying now. The trouble with all departments of the government is that no check of this kind is in effect. I am not against all civil service officials; not at all, but I do not want them to have a free hand. I want the principle of ministerial responsibility restored; when I say that, I use the king's English and everyone should know what I mean. It is essential that power given by the people should be checked by the people, through their representatives, but in order to do this, information is necessary. It would be in the interests of the department to spend two or three million dollars, if necessary, in order to see just where we stand with regard to pensions.
Any member of parliament or any citizen can make representations to the commission with regard to any case, but unfortunately very

Pension Act
31S3
often those representations are entirely disregarded. It is impossible, I regret to say, to make any representations to anyone on the pension commission. I have nothing against these gentleman personally, but they will not listen to anything. They are as stubborn as stone; you cannot argue with them. Here is a pitiful case, which should receive sympathetic consideration. No; the pension award is S3.75 a month. Another man may have had his lungs injured by shrapnel; he may have spent a long time in a hospital. To all appearances he is husky and strong. The commission do not know his condition, how sick he is; they say, "You are well. You are just a lazy fellow. You are all right. You do not need a pension." The man receives a message on a long sheet of paper, telling him to go back home; they suggest that he should go to work, as though they were passing judgment on his disposition instead of on his disability, which is altogether different.
I have the utmost sympathy for those men who were promised so much by the Union government from 1917 on. Those soldiers were told that they would get anything they wanted, that the land would be theirs and that they would be looked after by the government. Of course exaggerated statements were made at that time, which amounted to deceit with regard to these men. On the other hand, however, they had the right to expect fair treatment by our government.
I admit there have been men fairly treated; but though a hundred or a thousand men are treated well-and some of them have been treated too well-I shall never be satisfied while others receive none of the benefits they were promised. If there is one place where there should be no favourtism, no nepotism and no patronage of any kind, it is in connection with our soldiers, who make equal sacrifices. That is my humble view.
Then there is something else, Mr. Chairman; it is the absurd things that have been done. One of these is the preference which is given under other legislation to men who have been disabled, which means men who have pensions. I wonder whether all hon. members are familiar with that legislation, by virtue of which a man is considered disabled only if he has a pension. Take the case of a man who was fortunate enough to get a pension although he was not wounded, although he did not feel any pain or suffer any hurt. He receives a preference over another man who was disabled and who still feels the hurt of his wounds. I find this absurd, but that is the situation under sections 28, 29 and 30 of the Civil Service Act. Then the man who has a pension is given a preference over the returned man who has no
pension. That means there is a double preference. Many hon. members do not know this. For instance, if at a civil service examination a returned man who is in receipt of a pension, although he suffered no disability, obtains one hundred per cent while another returned man, who was wounded, obtains only enough marks to pass, it is the second man who is placed at the head of the list, at the expense of the first one. And if a civilian obtains one hundred per cent on a civil service examination, as against a returned man with only 70 per cent, the returned man goes to the head of the list. This is why the standard of the civil service is lower now, as everyone admits.
I want the soldiers to be well looked after by the state. One of the taxes which would become popular would be a tax for returned men; it would be a tax specified for the returned men; and everybody would pay that tax gladly as an honour and a tribute to those who have done so much. But now the taxes come from the melting-pot, and there is a limit to the payment of taxes. My idea is that the returned man should be well looked after for the simple reason that he deserves it. There should be a check made on the pensions paid, so that there may be no abuse, and so that the state would have to pay pensions to those deserving of them and who have not yet received them. There should be justice; there should be fairness.
I would give a last chance to the commissioners. I want them to have a free hand for six months, or until the house resumes its sittings, to see what they can do. I do not place any blame on the minister; he is my friend, and I have the greatest respect for him. I wish him good luck. But he knows that there are other considerations in the department. I would give the commissioners a free hand for six months, and I should like to know what will happen at the end of that time. Would we have an opportunity to examine each case on its merits? In addition, the commission should be empowered to make a check on every payment made from that branch of the department.
I do not appeal to the sympathies of hon. members, but I must point out that each case should be considered on its merits. When a man receives a wound, or a disability-any wound or any disability-his case should be considered with the greatest and deepest attention.
I hope everybody has accepted my remarks in the same spirit in which they have been given. In these dire times I want all to be as happy as possible. Of course it is impossible to promise Eden to all the returned men. But now we have another war to face, and
Pension Act

each man in each branch of the armed service has a right to expect justice. I hope all will get it.

subtopic: APPLICATION TO CERTAIN MEMBERS OF CANADIAN AND UNITED KINGDOM FORCES-CHANGES IN PRINCIPLE AND PROCEDURE
speechtext:
We must look at this matter realistically. Can Canada supply a comfortable standard of living to all her people, even in war time? I do not think there is an hon. member in the committee who will be sufficiently reckless with his reputation to say no. Very well, then; we will lay that down as the first principle. What do we mean by a comfortable standard of living? I do not believe the ordinary Canadian is thinking of comfort in the sense hon. members know comfort. The average person is asking for a sanitary house, wholesome food and adequate clothing. This bill, sir, does not and will not either directly or indirectly ensure those three essentials to large numbers of returned men, returned men's children and returned men's wives. I will challenge any hon. member to contradict my statement on that point.
Since the bill fails when gauged by those three simple tests, it must stand condemned in the eyes and in the minds of hon. members of the committee. It is one thing to say we cannot afford a thing; it is another thing altogether to face the facts as they are, and to say whether or not we can do a thing. To-day we hear from end to end of the Anglo-Saxon world discussions such as those in which we hear Dorothy Thompson engage.
I am not committing myself to Dorothy Thompson's views or associating myself with her in whatever plans she has, but certainly this lady has awakened the people all over this country to the fact that we fight and live on goods, and where the goods are, or where there are the means of producing them, we can have those goods and use them for whatever purposes we choose. Just as soon as these principles are laid down, then we are on the ground, we are on basic realities.
The minister implied that I had not studied the measure. I am afraid I have studied it a little too much and that is why I made the remarks I did; I am prepared to back up everything I said. Indeed, I will go a good deal further than I went and still I shall be

Pension Act
speaking moderately; I shall be only discharging my responsibility as a member of this house in whose constituency there are scores and scores, I believe hundreds and hundreds, of sufferers from the last war-sufferers not merely in the sense of pain or of mental disquietude but of anxiety and physical want. May I read a statement which was considered of sufficient significance in this connection to be embodied by the veterans' assistance commission in their report of 1937. It will be found at page 27. Hon. members are all familiar with it, but it will do our souls good to contemplate for a few moments the things that are said in that statement. I quote:
Sir Robert Borden addressed the Canadian fighting forces at Vimy Ridge in 1917 in words ascribed to him as follows:
"You are men actually facing the enemy day and night. You are suffering greatly from fatigue, over-strain and the lack of rest. The marvel of it is that men could undergo such a strain without breaking. But you have never yet broken, and history will appreciate that in days to come. You men are about to enter one of the most serious engagements that ever faced the Canadian corps. I cannot at this moment give any information as to where this attack will be staged, whether it be successful or not. It is to be borne in mind that it will not be an easy success. We feel confident that you will succeed where others failed, for you have never yet failed in anything you have set your hand to as a Canadian corps."
May I stop here to draw the attention of the committee to two things which I consider of vital importance. The first is that Sir Robert Borden acknowledged that these men had been under such a strain that the marvel was they were able to stand it. I ask whether anyone believes that any man can go through such a strain and still be the same kind of man he was before he went through it. The second important point is that these men have never failed. I will make that declaration solemnly on this floor to-day. These men never failed. The failures began when we took a hand in it as a government. I continue the quotation:
"You can go into action feeling assured of this, and as the head of the government I give you this assurance, that you need have no fear that the government and the country will fail to show just appreciation of your service to the country and empire in what you are about to do and what you have already done. The government of the country will consider it their first duty to see that a proper appreciation of your effort and of your courage is brought to the notice of the people at home, and it will always be our endeavour to so guide the attitude of public opinion that the country will support the government to prove to the returned man its just and due appreciation of the inestimable value of the services rendered to the country and the empire; and that no man-
Note these words:
-no man, whether he goes back, or whether he remains in Flanders, will have just cause to reproach the government for having broken with the men who won and the men who died.
May I now read what the veterans' assistance commission said:	'
Sir Robert, on behalf of the government, entered into a contract every whit as binding as that between Canada and the holder of victory bonds. In a certain sense the contract was more solemn. The victory bonds were after all pretty much a business transaction. The contract between Canada and her men going overseas reached beyond business into the realm of the ideal.
Those words were uttered. They are on record, and in the light of them I will ask the minister whether he thinks we have been just to our fighting men. I know he will feel we have not. He will argue that he has done a great deal for the benefit of the returned men. I will grant that. I was not discussing what the minister had done or what he had not done. The hon. member for Temiscouata a minute ago half slightingly-I wish to be fair to him-referred to these promises which the administration made between 1914 and 1917. Let us suppose they were exaggerated. It can be argued with equal justice that the high interest rates promised the people who bought victory bonds were exaggerated. But I ask you, sir, whether anyone wishes to modify those bonds or cut them down, or has done so up to the present time. The answer is either a significant silence, or no. Well, then, if we hold ourselves so rigidly to our contract with respect to victory bonds, why is it we have not held ourselves with equal rigidity to the contract we made with our men? We have not failed in our bond interest, nor have we repudiated any of our bonds as a Canadian government. I am aware that the committee knows all these things, but what amazes me is that the members of the government can do the things they do realizing that what I have read is true. Let me read to the committee a little statement which I believe is probably quite unbiased. It is reported on page 12 of the issue of May 1 of the Western Producer, under the caption "Mission worker tells of poverty in Saskatchewan." My object is to indicate to the committee how admirably we are fulfilling this pledge which Sir Robert Borden made.
Captain A. Hutchins of the Canadian (Anglican) church army describes conditions of poverty and want that exist among the settlers in his northern mission field in Saskatchewan.
He is speaking before the St. Johns W. A. of Saskatoon, presided over by Mrs. W. A. Ferguson, at its meeting in the parish hall on Tuesday afternoon. The reason why I
31S6
Pension Act

mention this is to indicate that there is no politics in it at all. It is possibly a fail-statement of facts and, therefore, very valuable.
He says:
I have seen the slums of London and our eastern cities, but I have never seen the abject poverty and want that exists among the settlers of northern Saskatchewan.
May I stop there for a minute to point out that when the hon. member for North Battler ford (Mrs. Nielsen) cried out against these conditions, she was rewarded by having members of this house call her a communist. I go on to read the report:
He was speaking of that block of bushland, measuring about thirty by thirty miles around Prairie River, approximately 200 miles north of Saskatoon. It is this block of land that he tours summer and winter as young missionary for the Anglican church.
In this vicinity is the old soldiers' settlement: Land which the government deeded to returned soldiers. These soldiers were city-bred watchmakers, shoemakers and craftsmen who had never lived on the farm. The result was chaotic. The hardier ones were able to pull through but the majority lost faith in the land and themselves. This section is hemmed in by forest and reserves. Names like Blighty, Somme, Caragana, Mosquito and Shady Lane tell their own story.
There is also in this section the land given to farmers who have moved north.
From here on we are unable to tell whether he is describing returned soldiers' families or the families of farmers who have gone north, but in either case these conditions are a great disgrace. I quote:
These farms are covered with bush and at best only twelve acres a year can be cleared. The families get little relief and there are from six to eight children in many homes. In one home with eight children that Captain Hutchins visited there was a girl eleven years old with only one garment and children of four and six who went about the house naked. In this home the stovepipe was made of lard tins placed together. The mother had six children of her own but when her neighbour was taken away, insane, she took the other family's two children into her poor home.
The schools are two room log affairs not large enough to accommodate the "awful lot of children" (as the captain expressed it) in this fi'ontier district.
I do not know what the ministers think about that, but I believe the future generation will certainly look back upon such conditions with deep regret. "Awful lot of children". Those were the finest men we have had in Canada and yet we do not bother to raise their children. We place no value upon children in this country 1 Apparently we do not need them any longer I The only ones who need children are the Italians, the Germans and the Japanese. We do not need any more. It is astonishing, is it not? Yet

that very tenor, that very thought is in this regulation which indicates that men are not to be rewarded for the children born after 1933. I consider that a terrible disgrace. That is one of the things we have done. What do the returned men themselves think about it? I may mention that I had the statement I am about to read under my hand when the minister made his scathing remarks a short while ago about the statement I made then. I intend to read from a statement put out by the York (E) veterans' social welfare club of 2209A Queen street east, Toronto, which city is claimed as being the most loyal in Canada.

We respectfully submit to you our humble representations, and pray that you will use your good offices on behalf of those who are suffering privation, semi-starvation, and continued degeneration as their reward for the service rendered by their husbands in the defence of Canada and all that our constitution so stands for.

"Disgraceful"? "Disgusting"? I would rather think so!
-bled and died, and as contrary to that for which our sons, and kin are so now prepared to die if called upon so to do.
We are respectfully of the opinion that British justice, and the right by statute of the individual is assailed which permits a commission to be judge, jury, and court of appeal at one and the same time, as at present operative, and which deprives the applicant the right as is said applicant's basic right, to appeal against such decisions of this body.
I am reading the next paragraph to indicate how calm this statement is. The minister replied that nothing was ever achieved by being extreme. Here is plenty of calmness, but apparently it did not get very far. I quote:
We do respectfully agree that in its composition, the pension statutes are all to the benefit of those for whom said statutes are compiled, but the entire benefit of said statutes are set aside when the whole power of interpretation and final decision of entitlements are vested in the commission as the sole body of adjudication and these said statutes are without value, when regulations as drawn up and operated by the Canadian pension commission are used to offset the benefits of said statutes.
'The hon. member for Temiscouata conveyed to me the impression that the blame for these adverse and hurtful regulations should be placed upon the pension commission.

In my opinion that commission is not responsible at all. The responsibility lies upon the instructions which they probably receive behind the cupped hand.

I do not think it is the Minister of Pensions and National Health; I do not think he is callous enough to do the things that are done. I refer to the statement made by the hon. member for Temiscouata. The evidence adduced here this afternoon is enough to condemn the whole pensions set-up in this country. speechtext:
When the committee took recess, I was endeavouring to show what the returned men and their dependents think of what is being done and what has been done as a result of the operation of the Pension Act. I have read one excerpt of a statement of one group of people in Toronto. I should like to read another letter. I am not sure whether, before doing so, I should apologize for the harshness of some of the expressions, but I will merely say that they are the words of a responsible group of people who are representing the men who served Canada in the last war.
Woodstock, N.B.
February 21, 1941.
Hon. Sir:
May we draw the following to your attention for your consideration in the light of present conditions,-
That the War Veterans' Allowance Act is a disgrace to Canada and an insult to the veterans and their dependents you can see from reading it over.
You must surely know that no helpless unemployable war veteran can live and keep a family on $40 per month. How is this spent? Rent, $25; milk, $5; wood, $10; total, $40. For food, clothing and medicine they must depend on charity. Is this what you have in store for those now serving?

subtopic: APPLICATION TO CERTAIN MEMBERS OF CANADIAN AND UNITED KINGDOM FORCES-CHANGES IN PRINCIPLE AND PROCEDURE
speechtext:
Usually the signature comes at the end of a letter: it does in this one.
The veteran's wife is forced to neglect her own home and family and work for others to help support the family of this helpless war veteran by washing, scrubbing, cooking or whatnot; and you send your gestapo around to see if this slave-wife has been working hard enough that you can deduct part of the veteran's allowance, and they are asked to keep a record of their earnings so that this can be done. Rent paid and 50 cents a day to live and keep a family, and you call yourselves men. We went through hell and could get no pension for our disabilities but dunged on for our sacrifice. We are still sacrificing and lost the things we fought for. We have slavery for our wives and poverty and rags for our families.
We demand the following changes in the War Veterans' Allowance Act:
Some may say that we are not discussing the War Veterans' Allowance Act; but I contend that, if the Pension Act were what it ought to be, there would be no need1 for a War Veterans' Allowance Act.
We demand the following changes in the War Veterans' Allowance Act:
1.	That the allowance be increased as follows: married men, $75 per month; single men, $35 per month.
2.	That an allowance be made for each child, as under the Pension Act.
3.	That the allowance be paid to the veteran's widow until she marries, as under the Pension Act.
4.	That the earnings of the slave-wife have no bearings on the veteran's allowance for his war disabilities.
The chairman of the board receives upon retirement the same amount as the allowance for five families of war veterans with five rents to pay, five homes to heat, twenty-five people to feed, and twenty-five people to clothe. Also to keep the children in school and taxes paid. Is this the kind of democracy we fought for? Why honour the dead and curse the living? Twenty-five people to be kept in poverty so that one may live in luxury. God save Canada. We want a square deal, nothing more, nothing less.
Yours respectfully,
P. M. Tamlyn,
I have purposely selected, Mr. Chairman, two of the many documents which have reached my desk, one from New Brunswick
Pension Act

and one from Ontario. I believe that these two provinces are ordinarily looked upon as among the most loyal provinces in the dominion. I regard these statements as of great significance indeed.
There may be only a few cases like this in Canada, as some men say, but the fact that there are any, in a land of such abundance as this, is a serious reflection upon the wisdom of the men who have governed and are governing Canada.
There is one matter which I believe altogether too few people appreciate. I have mentioned this once or twice already in this chamber. Only two or three days ago I received a letter from a man out in British Columbia. What he wrote was to this effect: "I have a 15 per cent disability, but that 15 per cent disability keeps me out of every kind of employment I seek to get. I might just as well be in gaol for all I can earn, because no one will hire me; and if I try to run a business for myself, I have not the strength to stand up to the strain. The result is that I am a one hundred per cent disability, but all the compensation I can get is for 15 per cent."
This difficulty arises from the fact that we are now in an age of abundance and have no need of the efforts of a great many of our people, suoh as we had twenty years ago. It is because the people in charge of the administration of this act, as well as those who drafted and framed it, did not realize this fact that they failed to appreciate the serious injustices which are visited upon the veterans by reason of the whole set-up through which we deal with our returned men. We are in an age of unemployment; and it would not matter if I had no disability at all, if I could not get employment I could not live, and if I could not earn my living I would immediately become an object of charity.
The same thing applies to the women. Only in the last few days there was in my office a woman from Toronto representing the war veterans' widows. This woman said', "I am sixty years old; I am strong and vigorous, but I cannot get work because no one will accept me for (work. The result is that I simply have no way of living." Let that fact impress itself upon the mind of every member of this committee and of every responsible person in Canada. Industries are now refusing offers to work by men over fifty years of age. One returned man told me on the streets of Ottawa two or three days ago-I did not have a chance to go and check with him- "I can go down to a certain park in Ottawa any day and find you fifty returned men, any one of whom can do carpentry work, but not one of whom will be given a chance to do that or any other kind of construction

job. All these men are strong enough to work, but merely because they are a little too old, they are not accepted." Let that fact be borne in mind in dealing with this whole situation.
The next thing is the difficulty of selling goods. I have a letter from a constituent of mine, a man who has settled on a farm as a result of his services in the last war. He says: "I have had a sufficiently difficult time to keep the wolf from the door and to keep up my payments. All during the depression I suffered and was in constant danger of losing my farm. Now, just as the depression is apparently passing, I am unable to sell my wheat. How can I possibly discharge my responsibilities financially? How can I save my farm?" I have not been able to find an answer to this question; I hope that someone in charge in Canada can.

What changes would the
hon. gentleman suggest in the new pension bill which goes much further than the old one?

I did not really come prepared to make suggestions as to what might be done, but I would extend the application of the Pension Act and the War Veterans' Allowance Act so that there would not be a needy sufferer in Canada either as a war veteran or a dependent of a war veteran. I do not mind seeing a war veteran go to work if there is work for him to do; but when there is no work he can do, then certainly something must be done about the matter. I was told about one man who lost his hand in the last war. I do not know what percentage of disability that gives him-15 per cent or thereabouts, I suppose. That man has a job as a postal official. He is able to make a living. But suppose he had not a post office job and had to be on a dairy farm; suppose he had to handle horses, or suppose he tried to get any one of a hundred jobs that one could name. How in the world could he get a job when no one would accept him? That man is as good as a total disability, because if he cannot get work that he can do, such as running an elevator or something of the sort, there is no hope for him. He certainly should be included within the War Veterans' Allowance Act or the Pension Act, so that he would not need to worry about a living. I believe I have laid down a principle there. I have not worked out the details, but I could do so if I had time. That answers the hon. member's question.
We are now facing another difficulty. It is becoming almost impossible for a man to establish a business, when we remember all the regulations and restrictions and taxes which are being imposed by the Minister of Finance.

Pension Act
At the same time there is a rise in the cost of living. I have not yet heard of a single case in which a veteran has been granted an increase in his allowance or pension by reason of the rise in the cost of living. Two or three times a bonus has been awarded to men working, to meet the increased cost of living; but nothing has been done for the veteran. Are we assuming that he has to cut down his standard of living in accordance with the rise in the price of goods? If so, how can we possibly justify ourselves?
Taxes are being applied to the veteran, and that again is raising his costs and increasing his difficulties. The sugar tax, the sales tax, all the other nuisance taxes of which we have an abundance in the country to-day apply to the veteran in a blanket fashion, with no provision or allowance or exception made whatsoever.
I have not heard up to the present time of any special provision being made to avoid having the soldier lose his farm. In Alberta or Saskatchewan, or in any of the western provinces where farmers have established farms and have been struggling to make a living, when the dominion government makes it so that they are unable to sell such wheat as they grow, and gives them a little less for the production of wheat than it costs to produce wheat, the dominion government has made no provision to prevent their creditors closing in on them.
Is it not high time we began to take cognizance of all the confounding difficulties that are developing round the veteran? When are we going to face facts in this house with respect to veterans?
Some will say it is impossible to do all these things. After I gave my last speech, there were several smart-Aleck newspapers in the country that made remarks about how easy it was for people like me to come here and say how the government should spend the people's money. The point is this: Let us come here and set forth what needs to be done and then let us find the money. People will say it is impossible to do this. I maintain it is not impossible to do it. The only reason why it is impossible is that we insist on controlling what we do physically by what we can do financially. We do not attempt to make what is physically possible financially possible.

What we needed was the impossible. Possible and impossible are all relative terms. What is impossible under one kind of organization, one sort of moral awakening, one sort of programme of leadership is perfectly possible under another type of organization, morale and leadership.
You are much better than she is.

I hope so, let her be as good as she might. Let it be borne in mind that we are growing richer as a result of the war, so far as our ability to produce is concerned. Every new factory established makes us richer. Every new increase in productive capacity makes us richer; for the riches of a country must be measured by the ability of that country to produce goods of all kinds. Therefore we are growing richer. We have a set of debts that are troubling us, but the productive capacity of the country is going to be here after the war if we have vision and wdsdom enough to make use of it instead of destroying it as we did during the depression. If we are getting richer physically, and shall continue to do so, why can we not devise some new way of dealing with these riches so as to allow the returned men both of the last war and of this war to participate in these riches?
Canada, as long as she will give patient consideration to a bill such as this, is yet far from playing fair with her soldiers, whether past, present or future. Great changes are due and must be made-changes in the provisions and purposes of the bill, changes in the administration of the bill. Only thus shall Canadians make financially possible what is physically possible for Canadians, and so keep faith with those to whom Canada is pledged.

It is not my intention to make a lengthy speech with reference to this bill. We should, however, bear in mind that its provisions are, I think, very generous. It should be remembered that in the last twenty years Canada has paid out over a billion dollars in pensions to those who served in the last war. That amount can come from only one source, namely, the general taxes of the people of Canada. There should be from time to time a general review of those cases that are receiving pension. It does not necessarily hold that because a man has been designated
Pension Act

as eligible for pension, he has a permanent disability, either partial or complete. In these days, with modern medical science and surgery, disabilities may obtain for a few years and be removed. That is the type of case which should be reviewed. I want it understood that I am in general accord with the granting of liberal pensions to deserving pensioners. But I am equally sure that there must be many people receiving pensions who are not as much entitled to them at present as when the pensions were awarded. The proof of that is that we have men enlisting in this war who are pensioners from the last war; they got a pension because they had some disability as a result of the last war, and up to the date of enlistment in the present conflict they have been receiving that pension and are receiving it now, yet they have been passed as A-l. Surely that is conclusive evidence that a number of these cases should be reviewed.
May I now say a word as to hospitalization. A pensioner is entitled to hospitalization if he is ill or has some disability which requires treatment. According to our present system the country is zoned, and pensioners within a certain district have to receive treatment in specified areas. For instance, in the Ottawa valley, the Ottawa hospitals, the civic hospital, and the general hospital, are the specified hospitals. I submit that throughout this section

and I have no doubt the same situation obtains in many other sections throughout the country-there are hospital facilities and men practising medicine and surgery who are competent to do the work that has t" be done, and to have these pensioners brought to a centre like Ottawa is added expense. I do not know whether that is a matter of the statute or of regulation; at all events it is one that should be remedied, to the benefit of both the pensioner and the institutions in smaller communities.
Another matter has to do with workmen's compensation. It appears now that a man who is perhaps a full-time pensioner, after a few years is in a condition physically to take a position in industry. Some accident happens to him and he comes under the workmen's compensation board. Under the provisions of that board in Ontario, any one who is injured in industry, after seven days' disability receives free hospitalization, free medical care and two-thirds of the wages he had been earning, with a minimum of $12.50 a week. If that man is a pensioner and is receiving one hundred per cent pension he goes in hospital and is attended, and in addition he receives from the workmen's compensation board free medical attention, free hospitalization and two-thirds of his wages. I understand that in [Mr. McCann.J
Ontario the practice has been to send the bill for the hospital to the Department of Pensions and National Health and it is paid by them. In my judgment that is not as it should be. That should be an obligation upon industry and upon the workmen's compensation board of Ontario, and should not be passed on to the federal authorities. I agree that that man is entitled to all the benefits of the Workmen's Compensation Act, but I see no reason why the cost should be passed on to the federal exchequer and come out of the taxes gathered by the federal government. I may be wrongly informed on that. I should like to have a word from the minister with reference to it.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health

There is, I assure my hon. friend, no right to pension conferred by the amending section. It was considered carefully by the committee, and I believe the opinion of the committee was that it was a fair and reasonable amendment.

Of course I understand the first point made by the minister, when he said that this does not confer an absolute right to pension. That question is left in the discretion of the governor in council. That is true as the bill is written, but does anyone believe for a moment that the government inserted this provision without having been asked to put it in for the benefit of some individual or individuals who are barred from getting a pension under the law as it is to-day? There is no doubt about it; this is adding to the service of someone time spent on a government board in the pension administration who to-day cannot get a pension, or who could not get a pension as large as is contemplated by this section. Otherwise this section would not be in the bill at all. Certainly it is no part of the general law of this country with regard to the returned soldier problem. This is special legislation on the face of it, and of necessity it must be for the benefit of one or more individuals. I have made some investigation into this, and I think it is true that it is for the benefit of one or more individuals. It is true that it is not mandatory on the government to pay this man this pension; but I venture to say that, if this section goes through, before the snow flies this gentleman or these gentlemen, whoever they are, will be in receipt of pension at the expense of the taxpayers of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: As I tried to intimate this afternoon, subsection 3 is a compromise between two points of view. One would be the application of the so-called insurance principle to all those serving in Canada, no matter in what capacity; the other would be the application of the "due to service" principle in Canada. This subsection is intended to meet a group of cases that may be on the border-line, and I think it involves two principles. One is that the injury, disease or aggravation has resulted in serious disability or death; the other is that the widow or children are in necessitous circumstances. Those are the two conditions involved; the one, a substantial injury, and the other, the matter of need. Hon. members who have followed the proceedings of the select committee will find that at page 407 of those proceedings practically the same provision was advocated by the spokesmen who appeared on behalf of the Amputations Association of Canada. I do not know if my hon. friend wants any further comment than that.

This afternoon I understood the minister to say that he thought the majority of the committee would have preferred a provision which would bring under the insurance principle all those men who were going to go overseas and do the fighting. That was also my impression of the wishes of the committee. Then the minister went on to say that it had been found impossible to draw up a section which would meet that wish. I suggest to the minister that it is only fair that the men who are going to do the fighting should be covered by the insurance principle. I am not urging that the men who will not be going overseas should be so covered, but I do suggest that the men who are going to do the fighting for Canada should be covered while they are in training here, waiting to go overseas. I would urge that the
Pension Act

minister have one more try at drawing up a section to meet that situation, instead of putting into the act an expedient which obviously will meet only a few border-line cases, and which is founded entirely on a hardship basis. I realize the difficulty of drawing up such a section, but I suggest that the minister allow this part of the bill to stand overnight and make one more attempt to draw up a provision that will be more inclusive in its application, and cover the men who are going to do the fighting for this country.

My hon. friend expressed in the committee the same view that he has expressed this evening; and it is equally true that the committee and its legal advisers explored every possible avenue in seeking a solution along the lines which were then advocated by the hon. member and supported by quite a substantial number of the committee. speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health

speechtext:
That means, in plain language, that the easy way out has been taken; because in a search for a formula to meet the obvious requirements of justice for these men the government were unsuccessful. They have found no formula. There must be a point in respect of all of those forces-the navy, the army and the air force-when it will be possible to say that a man is bound for overseas. The provision with regard to the navy is very broad in any event, because the definition of service in a theatre of actual war, so far as the navy is concerned, includes service on the high seas. That means, of course, that practically every man in the navy on board a ship, even on the Canadian coast, would be included.
As for the air force, perhaps for a period during training it is not known who are going overseas and who are not. But there comes a time when it should be possible for departmental officials in one department or another to say that such and such a man will go overseas. I suggest that the same thing should be possible for the army.
Surely we are not going to throw up our hands and fail to give these men adequate protection because so far it has been impossible to find a formula in the English language to cover them. I repeat my suggestion to the minister, namely, that he allow this section to stand overnight, and make one more attempt to work out a section which will meet the requirements.

I do not
quite appreciate the difficulty the minister has visualized and explained at some length. Does the difficulty lie in the acceptance of a principle or of a set of principles? I never have had any trouble in my practice or in my experience in clothing a principle with language which would be appropriate, intelligible and workable, if I could once define the underlying principle with which I was attempting to deal. I admit at once that I think it would be difficult to find one formula which would cover every class of case to which the minister has referred. I agree that that would be mechanically impossible. I suggest, however, that if the committee, the minister and the department could sit down together and define a certain set of principles covering each category, and have it flexible enough so that when a man departed from one position to another there could be agreement as to the principle of pensionability, and that this could be done at the exact time when a man could move from one category to another, there should be no great difficulty in finding a formula upon which proper administration could be worked out.
Is it suggested that the government's decision that the matter is hopeless, because, after all, that is the minister's position, is based on the theory that the department is of opinion that these men should not be pensioned? Let the minister come out in the open and tell the committee frankly whether it is the considered opinion of the department that men in the army, we shall say, such as have been described by the hon. member for Vancouver South, should not be pensioned at all. If that is the position, then let the minister say so. Could the minister say it?	_
If, however, there is a sincere desire that men in Canada who are training should be given some protection from public funds and under certain properly defined principles- not adhering strictly to the underlying principle, we shall say, of the Workmen's Compensation Act, but rather on the insurability principle, or the absolute principle to which reference was made to-day-I see no great difficulty in finding a formula. The same observations would be true with respect to the navy. I see no great difficulty there at all. The same would apply to the air force.
Some of the men may be in purely administrative positions. For instance, let us say that one young man is a very clever young man working as an accountant in a bank, and desirous of serving his country. Perhaps I can better illustrate my point by a specific case than by a general statement. Let ue
Pension Act

suppose that this young man. comes into the air force, and finds after enlistment, examination and preliminary training that he is not qualified to be an observer or a pilot. Possibly he is too old, or is not satisfactory for actual flying for some other reason. This young man may be transferred to the paymaster's branch. As a matter of fact, I have just such a case in mind. The man I am thinking about is doing wonderful work in auditing, and because of his ability efficiently to perform the service in which he is now engaged he has been promoted.
That man should not, in my opinion, have a pension. I would not be willing to pay him a pension. He is on leave of absence from the bank; and when the war is over, unless in the meantime he drops dead, he will return to his job and receive his promotions in the bank. Certainly he should not have a pension. On the other hand, however, there are large numbers of young men who have enlisted and are looking forward to going overseas.
The point at issue here is this: Should they have a pension if they are injured while training in Canada in anticipation of going overseas? If we can agree on the principle, then I say to the minister that with all the expert draftsmen employed by the government it should not be at all difficult to find a formula. It cannot be done in one formula, and the various categories and classes will have to be dealt with as they arise. I suggest that this is quite possible.
Much would have to be done by regulation. That is why on occasions authorities are given permission to legislate by regulation. They must do so to meet a great diversity of cases relating to one specific subject matter or substance. I say to the minister it would not be impossible for skilled draftsmen to meet such a position, and I must support the hon. member for Vancouver South in his suggestion that the position be reconsidered in the light of the plea which has been made.

I was not here this afternoon because I went to Petawawa camp, and therefore I am not familiar with the discussion that took place. I take it that that discussion was on the general principle of the bill, and I shall try to avoid any repetition. I should like, however, to make a few remarks on section 6. First of all, I wish to voice my appreciation of the very fair and efficient manner in which the chairman of the committee conducted its business and also of the services contributed to that committee by the chairman of the pension board. I think the minister has announced the fact that the report was not unanimous. I was not able to agree to a unanimous report because of certain sections in the bill which did not change the principle of the Pension Act. I thought there should have been amendments to correct certain injustices that exist in the act. Consequently my quarrel is not so much with the bill as with certain injustices which exist in the act and which have not been removed by this bill.
Generally speaking, I am in favour of this section. I believe all members will agree with me when I say that this section is a great improvement over the section first submitted to the committee, but it is not as broad as the section was prior to the order in council which was passed last May. At this time I wish to voice strong criticism of the practice of this government of passing orders in council that destroy certain acts which have been passed by parliament, especially when that action is taken during a session. It does not seem to me that that is the democratic way of doing things. At the present time we are engaged in a war between the democracies and the totalitarian states. I deplore the fact that this government is becoming more and more fascist in the way it is dealing with the enactment of legislation in this country.
My main objection to section 6 is the insertion of the word "serious' 'in respect of disability. That leaves a great deal to the discretion of the chairman of the pension board. I know some people will say that, in the past, section 21 of the Pension Act has not worked out satisfactorily. We must, however, remember that, in so far as section 21 is concerned, the words "meritorious" and "compassionate" are used, whilst in this case it is a question of need. Therefore I believe we can fairly well trust the pension board to deal with this matter in a sympathetic way. I do not blame the board for not having dealt with section 21 in a more satisfactory manner. The case was definitely defined in that section as to be of a "meritorious" character, and therefore their discretion was limited.

I agree with the last speaker, at least to some extent. This is a step in the right direction, but as I said in committee, I do not believe it goes far enough. While I have some sympathy with the minister in the difficulties he has encountered in drafting the section, I still believe that it could be improved. The difficulties go farther back; they are inherent, as I have indicated to the Minister of National Defence, in the organization of our Canadian armies. We have two distinct armies, and I believe it was the opinion of the committee that this country should feel a deeper responsibility towards those who are going overseas to fight than to the members of the reserve army. That being the situation, there is quite a distinction between the organization of our active service force and that of the reserve army. I have never felt satisfied that, if we should have a sudden call for large reinforcements, our reserve army would be suitable to take the place of those reinforcements. The difficulty with which the Minister of Pensions and National Health is confronted is that he cannot so draft the section as to provide for this condition. We wish to provide for all those who are training in this country at this time for active service. They are interlocked; members of the staff are transferred back and forth, so that the situation cannot be properly covered.

I see that the Minister of National Defence for Air is sitting with the Minister of Pensions and National Health; as we all know, the former is an expert on pension problems, having been previously minister of pensions and, I must say, a very good minister. speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health

There is the truth.

There is one difficulty that confronts me, and to illustrate my point I shall refer to two units that have recently been transferred to a section of the country from which the minister comes-Nanaimo. These men, notwithstanding anything the minister may say-and I am not casting reflections on the efforts of the committee-were enlisted twelve or fourteen months ago for overseas service. That was definitely intimated to them when they enlisted. Just before they left for the western coast they considered that they were part and parcel of the overseas units, and when this reaches them it does not fit in very well with the announcement we had on the radio to-night with regard to the urgent need for 32,000 men; for in a sense we have broken faith with these men, because all along they have considered themselves-and I know, because I visited the camps frequently-as a part of the overseas units.

Either a good many people are twisted in their thinking on this section, or I am. I am, therefore, going to try to find out. I cannot understand the reasoning of the hon. member for Vancouver South so far as this section is concerned. To begin with,
319S
Pension Act

any man serving in Canada at the present time is protected under this bill against anything that may happen to him in the course of his duties. He has complete protection.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Under subsection 2.

Exactly. If, as the hon. member advocates, complete protection for everyone in Canada who has enlisted for overseas is included, the provision is, in my opinion, restricted 50 per cent, compared with the section as now written, because by his suggestion protection would be given to a large number of people who hold office jobs and who have no intention of going overseas.
The hon. member misquotes me. I did not say everyone enlisting for active service. I said, in training for service overseas.

I would construe it as meaning in training for service overseas. On the other hand, the problem we are trying to deal with, and at which this clause is aimed, being a step in the right direction, is the safeguarding of those people who cannot protect themselves, the men serving in Canada. Such a man goes out and something happens to him not in the line of duty. He is not protected except under this clause, which gives protection to his family if they are in necessitous circumstances. In the final analysis, that is why pension laws are enacted. It is to protect those who stand in need of protection. If something happened to the man who left his widow $25,000 or $30,000 or $50,000, under the meritorious clause, if he had won medals, she was entitled to consideration. The man who left his wife destitute was entitled to none. This clause protects the very people who need protection at the present time, but if you word it as the hon. member for Vancouver South wishes to have it worded, unless a man is in training for active service overseas, the protection will not be given.
I can construe that in another way. In my opinion it means a lever for conscription. You are telling the man serving in Canada that unless he is prepared to volunteer for overseas service you are going to hold a gun at his head. In order to get full protection he must volunteer for overseas service. But you still leave without protection a large percentage of people whom you must protect under any pension legislation, namely, the family who are left without any means at all.
So far as I am concerned, after hearing this clause discussed in committee and studying it myself, and having some experience in pension matters, I regard this provision as a simplification of the problem we have to handle now TMr. Gillis.]
and in the aftermath of the war. It protects the man whom I have heard mentioned many times-the man who goes on leave and is killed. It cannot be related to his military functions and, in consequence, his family are left destitute. Under the old act nothing could be done for such a man; under the bill as the hon. member for Vancouver South would have it worded nothing could be done for him; but under this section there are discretionary powers in the chairman of the commission and he can do something in such a case. I may be stupid, or I may be twisted in my thinking, but that is how I see this particular provision. I cannot understand the other angle.

I should not like the hon. member to think I am against this subsection. I believe it covers a certain number of cases as it stands, and I do not wish to have them deprived of the rights they get here. At the same time, I suggest that there should be more ample provision for the other class, the men who are in training for service to do the fighting. I would not wish to be taken as wanting to take away the rights given here to the other groups.

Would the two ministers allow the section to stand until to-morrow and broaden it out? The government is looking for recruits, and this question is a vital point at the present time to a number of men. They want to know whether faith will be kept with them in the future, because with them, as I see it-and I have had a great deal to do with them-security is better than opulence, and they want to be assured of security. This is an important time, when every member has been asked to help in the coming campaign, which we trust will be successful, and I hope that nothing will be done to detract from its success. This is an all-important clause to service fighting men in training. I would respectfully suggest to the two ministers that something should be done to broaden out the clause and clarify it. This section deals with pensions for pulmonary tuberculosis. In my contact with a great number of veterans' cases for some yiears now, I have found that many of them were suffering from tuberculosis to a greater or lesser degree but that in many instances it was impossible for them to establish that their tuberculosis was due to the war. I have often thought, and I wish to say here, that very few doctors could say definitely that a man who during the great war stood daily in the trenches for weeks at a time up his knees in water, mud, blood and muck, and who later contracted tuberculosis, did not suffer from that disease as a result of his service in the great war. I have in mind the case of two brothers who came from Scotland. They came from a strong, rugged, healthy family in the highlands, and following the war both contracted tuberculosis. subtopic: REGULATIONS CONTROLLING THE BUYING OF WILD ANIMALS AND SKINS FROM INDIANS

speechtext:
Hon. T. A. CRERAR (Minister of Mines and Resources) moved the second reading of Bill No. 24, to amend the Indian Act.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Vien in the chair.
On section 1-Regulations controlling the buying of wild animals and skins from Indians.

subtopic: REGULATIONS CONTROLLING THE BUYING OF WILD ANIMALS AND SKINS FROM INDIANS
speechtext: This bill has not previously been before the committee of the whole?

subtopic: REGULATIONS CONTROLLING THE BUYING OF WILD ANIMALS AND SKINS FROM INDIANS
speechtext: No.

subtopic: REGULATIONS CONTROLLING THE BUYING OF WILD ANIMALS AND SKINS FROM INDIANS
speechtext: Would the minister make just a brief explanation? I do not believe I have had an opportunity of looking at this bill.

subtopic: REGULATIONS CONTROLLING THE BUYING OF WILD ANIMALS AND SKINS FROM INDIANS
speechtext:
When the bill was first introduced I made a brief explanation of its purpose. It is intended to provide a measure of protection to Indians in the more remote parts of the country in the sale of their fur catch. Practices have developed, particularly in recent years, whereby traders, often more or less unscrupulous in character, journey to the remoter reserves, usually by aeroplane, at the time the Indians have their fur for sale. The Indian is not fully aware of the value of his fur, and the result is that often he disposes of it at prices very much below what it is worth. It is sought by this measure to bring such trading under proper control, by providing that the governor in council may, on the recommendation of the Indian affairs administration, create regulations which shall cover such traders, and under the regulations permits to trade will be provided before such traders can go to these remote reserves and do their bargaining with the Indians. It is intended, further, that the regulations shall provide that traders shall make a report to the Indian affairs administration of the furs they purchase and of the price they have paid

Export of Game
for them. In that way we can bring about a measure of control which to-day is very badly needed.
The importance of this measure will be apparent to the committee when I say that practically one-third of the Indian population of Canada, which now numbers approximately 118,000 or 119,000, lives in the more remote parts of the various provinces, particularly Quebec, Ontario, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia, and in the Northwest Territories. These Indians have no means of subsistence other than their fur catch. It is consequently to them, and:, I might add, to the government, a matter of great importance that as far as possible they shall secure the full value of their fur catch.

subtopic: REGULATIONS CONTROLLING THE BUYING OF WILD ANIMALS AND SKINS FROM INDIANS
speechtext: They are supposed to be self-supporting?

subtopic: REGULATIONS CONTROLLING THE BUYING OF WILD ANIMALS AND SKINS FROM INDIANS
speechtext: In order, as the leader of the opposition has interjected, that they may become as far as possible self-supporting. To the extent that that can be brought about, their dependence upon government assistance in the way of relief is reduced. That, briefly, is the purpose of this measure.

subtopic: REGULATIONS CONTROLLING THE BUYING OF WILD ANIMALS AND SKINS FROM INDIANS
speechtext:
I have no intention of delaying the measure because we are going to 'adjourn in a moment. On the face of it, this is a very fair proposal. It is intended, of course, to assist the Indians by preventing unfair dealings. I am just wondering whether in line 9 of the bill, in view of the minister's explanation and in view of the explanatory notes, and the provisions of sections 40 and 41, the word "prohibit" is necessary, because the whole context looks to control, not to prohibition. It seems to me, having regard to what has been said, that the section might read:
The governor in council may make regulations to control the buying or otherwise acquiring from any Indian. . . .
The word "prohibit" does not seem to be consistent with the text of the section or intended to be in the section. According to the explanatory note, there is provision now under sections 40 and 41 of the Indian Act to "prohibit the buying or acquiring from any band or irregular band of Indians or from any Indian of any cattle, other animals, grain, root crops or other produce on reserves" in certain provinces "without the written consent of the Indian agent." This amendment does not purport to go that far. I suggest that the draftsman has unnecessarily inserted the word "prohibit," because apparently it is not intended to prohibit; it is intended to control. The regulations visualized by the succeeding portions of subsection 1 are regulations looking to control, not to prohibition.

subtopic: REGULATIONS CONTROLLING THE BUYING OF WILD ANIMALS AND SKINS FROM INDIANS
speechtext: Practically the same provision obtains now on certain reserves. Indeed, I believe that on all reserves in the prairie provinces, Indians who acquire property in the way of cattle or horses are prohibited from selling them except under conditions laid down under the act. I do not think any harm will be done by leaving the clause as it is. I can scarcely imagine circumstances where prohibition would be enforced; but there might be a trading company, for instance, whose practices had become so notoriously bad that an order would be issued to the effect that they could no longer, or for a certain period, trade with a certain band of Indians.

subtopic: REGULATIONS CONTROLLING THE BUYING OF WILD ANIMALS AND SKINS FROM INDIANS
speechtext:
Then, of
course, under section 42A (1) the agent just withholds his permit. That would take care of that situation.

subtopic: REGULATIONS CONTROLLING THE BUYING OF WILD ANIMALS AND SKINS FROM INDIANS
speechtext: Sections 40 and 41 entirely prohibit the buying or acquiring from any band or irregular band of Indians of any cattle or other animals, grain, roots and other commodities.

subtopic: REGULATIONS CONTROLLING THE BUYING OF WILD ANIMALS AND SKINS FROM INDIANS
speechtext:
Without
the written consent of the agent.

subtopic: REGULATIONS CONTROLLING THE BUYING OF WILD ANIMALS AND SKINS FROM INDIANS
speechtext:
I have not looked up in
Hansard the discussion which took place when these sections were incorporated in the Indian Act. I believe it is a fair presumption that they were placed there to put a ban on traders who might persistently and systematically be defrauding the Indians. I should prefer to have the section remain as it is. The committee may rest assured that the administration will be wisely carried out.
I have an amendment to subsection 5 of section 42A. Subsection 5 of that section reads:
Every order made by the superintendent general under the provisions of this section shall be published in the Canada Gazette.
Regulations will be promulgated to give effect to the act, and I think it is desirable that the regulations should also be published in the Gazette. I will therefore ask my colleague to move the necessary amendment.

subtopic: REGULATIONS CONTROLLING THE BUYING OF WILD ANIMALS AND SKINS FROM INDIANS
speechtext:
I move that subsection 5 of section 42A be amended by inserting, at its beginning, the words: "The regulations made by the governor in council and." The subsection will then read:
The regulations made by the governor in council and every order made by the superintendent general under the provisions of this section shall be published in the Canada Gazette.

Amendment agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.
